en: Preface to the *Linjian Lu* by Hong Juefan,
composed by Xie Yi of Linchuan.
Hong Juefan attained the samādhi of mastery.
The Elder Yun’an was thus able to sport freely within the realm of calligraphy and ink; even his sighs and coughs became literary compositions.

Whenever he engaged in spirited conversation with eminent recluses of the forest, the topics were invariably the noble conduct of venerable masters, the bequeathed instructions of the monastic communities, the subtle purports of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the refined discourses of worthy scholars and gentlemen. Upon acquiring each such matter, he would record it.
He recorded them immediately. Over the course of nearly ten years, he collected more than three hundred matters. Among those who followed him was the venerable Benming;

though his outward manner appeared simple and casual, he was inwardly extremely refined and quick-witted. During the intervals between his periods of seated meditation, he divided these records into upper and lower fascicles and titled them the *Línjiān Lù* (Records from the Forest).
Because the records were made according to their chronological sequence, he did not arrange them by antiquity.
I have now arranged them in sequence so that they may be read with ease during conversation rather than requiring forced effort;

thus, the text flows gracefully and simply, devoid of any sense of difficulty or hardship. Everyone knows that Master Ming possesses this collection, and wherever he travels, those who come to borrow it gather like a market.
Fearing that the calligraphy might fade and the transcriptions become erroneous, Ming [acted accordingly].
It has been carved upon wooden plates and requested that I compose a preface to ensure its longevity for future generations.

I maintain that the composition of this work provides benefit to the religious teachings, much like fine grain in a year of famine or silk and cotton in a cold winter; how could it require my preface before being transmitted?
I wish to entrust this work to posterity so that it may endure imperishably; this is why I would otherwise have preferred to remain silent.
Indeed he was capable. In the past, Yue Guang excelled at refined discourse but was not skilled in writing. He requested Pan Yue to compose a memorial for him;
Yue first drafted two hundred words to express Guang’s own intent. Pan Yue then organized and refined them, resulting in a masterpiece. People of the time all said:
"If Yue Guang had not relied on Pan Yue’s pen, and Pan Yue had not relied on Yue Guang’s insight, this beauty could not have been achieved."
Indeed. Now, as for what Juefan speaks with his mouth and records with his pen, he possesses the excellence of both these sons. Why is this?
Generally, among literary men, those who possess wondrous insight do not necessarily possess fine talent; those who possess fine talent do not necessarily possess wondrous insight.
Only those who embody the Way have shed all attachments and views, in whom stillness and movement are both harmonized, and whose minds are like clear mirrors that reflect whatever they encounter.
Matters were thus resolved. Therefore, I spoke freely and wrote as my pen moved; there was nothing that was not true.
Thus, is it not because Juéfàn embodies the Way that he possesses the excellence of both these sons?
It is for this reason that I know a scholar must understand the Way. Juéfàn’s name is Huìhóng; he is a native of Jūnyáng and currently resides in Línchuān.
At Beijingde Chan Monastery.
This was written at the request of Lord Zhu, Grand Master for Honorary Attendance at the Xianmu Pavilion. Preface on the first day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Daguan era.
From the *Linjian Lu* (Record of the Forest) by Hong Juefan of Shimen:

Chan Master Xiaoshou of Xingjiao Temple in Hangzhou initially followed National Teacher Tiantai Shaokang. While engaged in communal labor (*pǔqǐng*), he attained awakening upon hearing a piece of firewood fall.
He composed a verse, saying: "Striking down is not another thing; Spreading across and intersecting is not dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—"

The Dharma King’s body was fully revealed; the National Preceptor merely nodded in acknowledgment. When he began teaching the Dharma, the monastic disciples vied with one another to honor his dignity.

When Wang Gong, the Palace Aide and Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, went out to govern Qiantang, he went to pay his respects to Shou. Upon reaching the lakeside, he dismissed his retinue of attendants.
He walked alone up to the meditation hall. Huishou was just then basking in the sun, wrapped in his coarse woolen robe, appearing entirely unperturbed.

Suddenly seeing him, he asked, "What is your surname, sir? The Duke replied, "I follow the surname Wang. Huishou immediately bowed to him. He pushed aside his rush-cushion, spread it on the floor, and sat down.

They conversed and laughed for the entire day before the Duke departed. When the disciples saw Huishou, they reproached him, saying, "That was a royal official who came; why did you not pay him due respect?"
"Ritual propriety is that upon which this entire assembly depends; it is no small matter.
The next day, when the Prince arrived again, the monks struck the great bell and welcomed him with ten thousand fingers raised. However, Shou stepped forward and stood beneath a pine tree.

When the Prince saw him from afar, he descended from his carriage, took hold of his hand, and said, "Why do you not greet me as you did on the previous day? Why have you suddenly adopted such formalities?"
Yes. As he walked along, Shou looked to his left and right and said, "The Vice Minister may indeed obtain it, but what about the Abbot’s anger?
His natural disposition was thus pure and refined; he was truly a mountain-dweller in the true sense of the word.
Chan Master Baiyun Yuan had a free and unrestrained spirit. When he was young, he traveled through the region of Xiang.
At that time, Chan Master Hui had recently come from Yangqi to reside at Yun’gai. Upon seeing him, Hui marveled at him; they would converse until late every night.
One day, Hui suddenly asked, "Whose disciple did you become when you shaved your head? He replied, "The Venerable Yuru of Chaling. Hui said, "I have heard that when he crossed a stream..."
Xuefeng said, "This verse you have composed is truly extraordinary. Can you recite it? Zhaodu immediately recited it: "I possess a divine pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil.
Today, the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating ten thousand peaks of mountains and rivers.

Hui laughed loudly and departed. Zhaodu stood there in astonishment, looking around him; he could not sleep the entire night. The next day, he requested to enter the master’s room to consult him further.
At that time, it was the beginning of the year. Fayan said, "Did you see the fox that was howling last night?
Zhaodu replied, "I saw it. Fayan said, "In this matter, you are one step behind him. Zhaodu was greatly startled and asked, "What do you mean by this?
Fayan said, "He loves being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. Thereupon, Zhaodu attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words.

The Elder Yuan of Wei-fu, of the Avataṃsaka school, addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities; it is present in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
in drinking tea and eating meals; in speaking and questioning one another; and in all that is done and enacted, in every movement of thought and stirring of intention.
Yet, even this is not it. He further said: "The times are now in decline; among people, few reach the age of sixty or seventy. You..."
Those who have entered my Dharma have not yet stabilized their practice; already three or four decades have passed. Before long, decline and illness will arrive.
When decline and illness arrive, old age arrives; when old age arrives, death arrives. How much further is it before that? Yet you still indulge your whims.
Why do you not spend the first, middle, and last watches of the night in pure stillness? When Lord Wen Lu was stationed at Beiping, Master Yuan came to visit him.
He took his leave. Lu Gong said, "The Dharma Master is old; where are you going? He replied, "I am going to enter parinirvāṇa.

Lu Gong laughed, thinking it was a joke, and watched him return. Later, he spoke to his sons and younger brothers, saying, "His spiritual resonance is profound and steady; his speech and laughter possess true flavor."
He was truly an extraordinary monk. A messenger was sent to observe him, and indeed he entered *parinirvāṇa*. The people were greatly astonished and marveled at this for a long time.
When it came to the cremation, [the Master] went in person to witness it. He placed a lapis lazuli bottle before the seat and made this vow:

"If the Buddha-dharma is truly efficacious, may the *śarīra* fill my bottle. As soon as he finished speaking, smoke descended from the sky and entered the bottle. When the smoke vanished, the *śarīra* appeared.
This was his aspiration. From this time forth, Lord Lu devoted himself with utmost sincerity to the Inner Canon, regretting only that he had come to know it too late.
Chan Master Shi of Qixian was a native of Jianyang. He was a successor of Master Chang of Baizhang. By nature he was lofty and simple;

he disciplined himself with rigorous strictness, never failing to observe the rules of decorum in his conduct. In his later years, he read through the Tripitaka three times. Fearing that reading while seated was not sufficiently reverent, he would instead stand while reading.
He would recite and practice while wearing it. When Master Nanchuan of Huanglong first traveled to seek teachers as a youth, he followed him for many years;
thus, much of what Nanchuan did throughout his life was modeled after him. He once said, "The Abbot of Qixian must have come from among the devas and humans;
he is a beacon for the monastic community. Chan Master Xuedou Xian once came from Mount Huai to rely upon him, but they did not harmonize, so he then composed [the following]:

He departed after composing a poem on Lion Peak, saying: "Perched upon the earth and spanning the void, its momentum never ceases; How could its claws and fangs ever deign to mingle with the common flow?
Heaven ordained it to be born atop a thousand peaks; Were it not for the clouds to support it, it would have no way to show its head."
Li Zao’s *Guoshi Bu* states: When Duke Cui Zhao asked the Daoist practitioner Faqin of Mount Jingshan, "May your disciple leave the household life?
Faqin replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something performed by generals or ministers. Duke Zhao sighed in admiration of these words.
Zan Ning composed a biography of Faqin that runs to nearly a thousand words; even for the death of a single cock that crowed at dawn, he recorded it.
Yet this was not equal to that. Why?
Because Chan Master Da-jue (Lian Gong) was revered by Emperor Ren-miao for his virtue and character; the world yearned for his dignified presence.
His dwelling and personal belongings could have been transformed into a magnificent monastery, yet he did nothing of the sort—save for [his establishment] in the capital.

To the west of this was a vihāra that could accommodate only about a hundred people. When the old man Xun Qian, who resided at Qixian, was summoned for official business by the district magistrate, he donned his commoner’s clothes and hurried to take refuge with Liaan.
Liaan received him in the main hall while occupying himself in a side room, observing the etiquette of a disciple with great reverence.
When high officials and nobles came to visit, they all found this strange; Liaan explained the situation to them in full detail and...
He said, "In my youth, I once sought the Way from Master Shun. Now, I ought not to allow the difference between our monastic attire and appearance to divide my mind.
Those who heard this sighed in admiration. King Ren (Ren-miao) took note of this and granted Shun permission to shave his hair again, whereupon he returned to reside at Xie Mountain.
When Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang was still a commoner, Emperor Wuzong detested him for his virtue and repeatedly sought to have him killed. The eunuch Qiu Gongwu protected and preserved him.
As the situation became desperate, Gongwu shaved his hair and made him a bhikṣu, allowing him to travel freely. Consequently, he visited and admired many famous mountains throughout the empire.
Upon reaching Hangzhou, he met the Chan Master An of Yanguan, who was a high-ranking disciple of Mazu of Jiangxi.

The younger brother, upon seeing him once, marveled at his extraordinary nature and treated him with exceptional kindness. Consequently, Emperor Xuanzong retained him for a long time at Yanguan Temple; when the Emperor ascended the throne, [he continued to favor him].
I longed to see him, yet Master An had passed away long before. Previously, Emperor Wuzong had utterly destroyed our teaching, but by this time it was being restored once more.
Although the flourishing or decline of the Dharma depends upon the times, how can we know that his efforts were not brought about by Master An?
Master Chou Wu’s virtue was no less than that of the Han dynasty’s Bing Ji, yet the *Xinshu* (New History) neglects him, recording only Ban [Gu].
Ban’s account appears in the *Biographies of Master An Chan*. It is truly lamentable. There was once a eulogy for his portrait which said:
"Having already regarded the world as equal to motes of dust, The body is but empty vanity, a dream within a dream. Do not say that the dragon-like countenance allows for discrimination;
Thus, with the divine eye, one recognizes the celestial being."
Zan Ning composed the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*, organizing them into ten categories. To place the study of doctrine (*yixue*) at the very top is already laughable.

Furthermore, he lists Chan Master Yantou Huo under "Austere Practice" and Chan Master Zhijue Shou under "Promoting Merit," yet although the Great Master Yunmen was the sovereign among monks and lived at the same time as them, Zan Ning ultimately fails to record him. Why is this?
When Master Chan Chen of Changsha encountered the death of a monk, he stroked the body with his hand and said, "Great assembly, this monk has truly acted as a guide for you all to deliberate upon.
Do you understand? He then spoke a verse: "Not a single dharma before one's eyes, Nor a person present in that very place.
The vast and boundless diamond essence— Neither false, nor real. He further said: "If you do not recognize the diamond essence..."
Yet this is called "dependent origination. Throughout the ten directions, all is true quiescence; who is there, and who is practicing?
Master Xuefeng, upon seeing a deceased monk, also composed a verse: "Bowing the head, one does not see the earth; Lifting the face, one does not see the sky.
If you wish to know the adamantine body, Just look before the skull. Xuansha said: "Right before the deceased monk is precisely *bodhi* encountered at every turn."
The divine light extending ten thousand *li* is the mark behind the crown. A monk asked Fayan, "What is the Bodhi that meets the eye before a deceased monk?
He replied, "It is right before you. The monk asked again, "Where does he go after passing away? He replied: [He replied: "He goes to where the wind blows and the clouds drift."

"When has a deceased monk ever undergone the process of *qiānhuà* (transformation/departure)? Jin asked. "What can be done about the present moment? [Zhaozhou] replied, "You do not recognize the deceased monk.
Among the venerable masters of recent times, none have again used this principle to instruct people; only Master Huìtáng occasionally brought it up."
He composed a verse for the day of National Teacher Nanyue’s parinirvāṇa, saying: "On the seventeenth day of the third month last year, One night, the spring wind shook the abbot’s quarters.
The three-cornered qilin entered the sea; Only the crescent moon remains, emerging from the heart of the waves.
Truth does not conceal falsehood; the crooked cannot hide the straight. Who will join me in this snow-song? Those with true resonance through the ages are found this very day. Furthermore:
It is said: "The person who departed in the past is that very person today; yet today, as before, that person does not return.
Since they do not come now and did not go then, white clouds and flowing waters drift on in empty vastness. Who says the scale and ruler are level? Within the straight there is still the crooked.
Who says the principles of things are uniform? Planting hemp, one still harvests millet. Piteous are those people who rush about under heaven; six times six is originally..."
36. Chan Master Nan resided at Jicui. At that time, he would ask his students about such phrases as "the Buddha’s hand," "the donkey’s feet," and "original conditions.

Although many responded, Master Nan would close his eyes as if entering meditative absorption, never once affirming or negating their answers. The students would depart in haste, ultimately unable [to resolve the matter].
Because one knows what is right and what is wrong, the world calls this the "Three Gates" discourse. In his later years, he composed three verses himself;
I shall now record only two of them: "My hand and the Buddha’s hand are raised together; Zen practitioners, take this directly.
In the place where there is no movement of spear or shield, one naturally transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs. My feet and the donkey’s feet walk side by side; every step accords with the Unborn."
It arises. One must simply wait for the clouds to part and the sun to appear; only then will this Way be able to unfold in all directions.
Zen Master Yungai Zhi once said to me: "In the past, when I entered Huangbo Monastery again and reached Fanggan, I saw a monk coming from the mountains.
I asked him, 'Regarding the words of the Three Barriers, how have you brothers been discussing them lately? The monk replied, 'There is a saying that is truly marvelous. It can be... [text truncated]
"Jiàn-yì, what is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? He replied, "Playing the lute under the moon. Or he said, "Holding an empty bowl on a distant road. "What is my foot like a donkey’s foot?
He replied, "A heron standing in the snow is not the same color. Or he said, "Treading on falling flowers in an empty mountain.
"What is your place of birth-connection (*jāti-pratibandha*)? He replied, "I am a person from such-and-such a place. At that time, [the Master] teased him, saying, "The former..."
Once, while traveling, someone asked the Elder, "What is the meaning of 'the Buddha's hand,' 'the donkey's hoof,' and 'the conditions of birth'?
Should you respond to this by saying, "On a distant road, you hold an empty bowl"? Or should you respond by saying, "The heron standing in the snow is not of the same color"?

If you respond with both, then the Buddhadharma becomes muddled; if you choose one over the other, then the function of the teaching becomes lopsided. That monk stared straight ahead without speaking.
I said to him: "Regarding what Xuefeng spoke of the ultimate point—when Chan Master Jia Shan first resided at Zhulin Temple in Jingkou, he ascended the seat. A monk asked, 'What is the Dharma-body?
He replied, 'The Dharma-body is formless. [The monk asked again,] 'What is the Dharma-eye? He replied, 'The Dharma-eye is flawless. At that time, Dao...
I was laughing among the assembly. Baizhang saw me from afar and, descending from his seat, asked, "Venerable sir, you were just now laughing;
what was it that made you laugh? Daowu replied, "I laughed because the Master, though traveling the same path as others, lets his straw sandals fall where they will. Baizhang said, "..."
"Could you tell me where he is? He replied, "I do not know how to say. [Zhaozhou] said, "In Huating, Xiu Prefecture, there is the Boatman Monk;
you may go to see him. Consequently, Zhaozhou disbanded his assembly and went there. The Boatman asked, "Virtuous One, which monastery have you recently been staying at?"
The monk replied, “If it were a temple, it would not be dwelling; if it were dwelling, it would not be a temple. The boatman asked, “If it is not a temple, what does it resemble?
He replied, “It is not a dharma within the reach of the present moment. The boatman asked, “Where did you learn this? He replied, “It is not something reached by the ears or eyes.
The boatman laughed and said, “A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. Alas! In the monasteries of today...

The Master of the Forest received disciples who, as a rule, strictly prohibited intellectual understanding and cast away all that was profound and subtle; they sought only direct questioning and direct answering.

If something did not exist, they spoke of its non-existence from beginning to end; if it did exist, they spoke of its existence from beginning to end. Even the slightest deviation was termed "mad interpretation.
Had the Boatman heard this, would he have been merely a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas? Viewed from this perspective, [the situation is clear].
It is not merely a matter of failing to awaken well; it is also a matter of failing to doubt well.

One who doubts well must reflect upon the occasions of awakening during the transmission of the Dharma by the thirty-three patriarchs. Their words remain extant, and all can be investigated through principle and understood through wisdom.
Yet, as for the various great masters from Shitou of Jiangxi onwards, who responded to things through the application of their spiritual mechanisms—observe their questions.
Answer: It is vast and boundless, making people drowsy as they sit. Is its Way different from that of the various patriarchs? If it were different, one would have succeeded to their Dharma;
if it were not different, then why are the words spoken so different? Therefore, we know that the Great Master Linji said:

"In general, when discussing the vehicle of the school, one must have the three mysteries within a single phrase, and the three essentials within each mystery. To possess both the mysteries and the essentials—"
This is precisely what is being clarified here. It is lamentable that those who do not understand point to this as mere "establishment of a school" or as expedient speech for the occasion.
Chan Master Tiānyī Huái taught the Dharma on Mount Huái; he changed his teaching seat three times, and his students followed and honored him until his Way became manifest.
Nevertheless, he did not yet dare to announce his name to Xuědòu. Xuědòu already marveled at him. There was a monk who recited...
His message concluded by saying: "It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water.

The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no thought of retaining the shadow. Upon reading this, he struck his thigh in lamentation and immediately dispatched someone to offer him consolation.
Daohuai then dared to send a single letter, merely inquiring after his health. Zen Master Zhēnrú of Mount Wèi had been a disciple of Zhēndiàn Xiōng for the longest time.
The monastic community was aware of this; yet, when receiving guests, they never spoke a single word regarding the matters of their past experiences or learning.
On the day of their parinirvāṇa, they would simply unfurl their portraits and offer tea and fruit as an offering. These two great elders possessed a vision that reached far beyond the ordinary.
To withdraw and excuse oneself on the grounds of being "cool and thin" (insignificant) in order to admonish later students can be called an excellent way of extolling one's master.
When Master Yun’an was residing at Dongshan, a monk asked:

"The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states that the afflictions of the ground of ignorance are themselves the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of all Buddhas, which all sentient beings inherently possess. It is only because..."
The essence of wisdom has no inherent nature and no dependence; it cannot realize itself, but realizes only by encountering conditions.

Furthermore, how can the afflictions of the ground of abiding ignorance become the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas? This principle is extremely profound and mysterious, utterly difficult to comprehend.
Yun’an said: "This is most clear and easy to understand. At that time, a boy was just sweeping; he called out to him, and the boy turned his head.
Yun’an pointed at him and said, "This is not the Immovable Wisdom (acala-jñāna). But tell me, what is your Buddha-nature?
The boy looked left and right and departed in bewilderment. Yun’an said, "This is not the affliction of the dwelling-place (bhūmi-kleśa).

If you can realize this, you will become a Buddha this very moment. Furthermore, he once asked a lecturer, "When a fire disaster breaks out, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all consumed by the flames."
"Everything is exhausted; the world is empty and void. Is this so? He replied, "The scriptures have clear explanations. How could there be any reason for it not to be so?
Yun'an said, "Where would you place all these ashes? The lecturer’s tongue was large and dry; he laughed and said, "I do not know.
Yun'an also laughed loudly and said, "What you have lectured upon is merely the words on paper. This is the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
His discernment was such that his answers transcended the expectations of others, while his questions left scholars breathless.
Possessing innate wisdom that required no teacher, he could not be matched by worldly intelligence; he was truly a patron of the Dharma for this age.
The Second Patriarch served the Great Master with diligence for many years, even going so far as to stand in the snow and sever his arm; yet Bodhidharma addressed him with but a single word.
Niu-tou Lan-rong practiced "lazy Chan" in the depths of the mountains, having no initial intention to seek renown, yet the Fourth Patriarch went to him in person to preach the Dharma.
There must surely be a profound purpose behind the way the Patriarchs related to their teachers and disciples.
The *Tanyuan Ji* (Garden of Talk) by Yang Wen Gong records a prophecy concerning future events inscribed on a copper plaque by the śramaṇa Baozhi, which states:
"A true man shall appear in Jichuan; opening his mouth and drawing his bow to the left, his sons and grandsons shall endure for ten thousand myriad years.
The Zhongzhu of Jiangnan named his son Hongji; the various sons of Qian Liu of Wuyue all had names beginning with the character "Hong," as if anticipating this prediction.

He responded accordingly, and it so happened that the taboo name of King Seonjo coincided with this. Furthermore, the record states: Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty destroyed all bronze statues to cast coins.
He said to his ministers, "In Buddhism, it is held that even one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain are not spared if they may benefit sentient beings;
how much less would one cherish a bronze statue? The Great Compassionate One (Dabei) of Tongzhou was extremely efficacious. It should...

He struck and destroyed it; with an axe, he struck its chest and carved through it. Taizu personally witnessed this event. Later, when Emperor Zong campaigned northward, he suffered from a carbuncle that broke out on his chest.
Everyone considered this a karmic retribution. Consequently, Taizu came to place great faith in the Buddhist teachings.

Ou-yang Wen-chung Kung’s *Hui-t'ien Lu* (Record of Retirement to the Fields) records at its outset that when Taizu first visited the Imperial Monastery (Sang-kuo Ssu), he questioned the Chief of the Monastic Registry (Seng-lu).
"Is it permissible to prostrate before the Buddha? Ning replied, "I do not prostrate. When asked the reason for this, Ning said, "One does not prostrate before a present Buddha;
one prostrates before a past Buddha. Consequently, this became the established rule. The records of both these gentlemen contain profound meaning; they were certainly not made lightly.
I have heard that a gentleman delights in doing good with others. Even regarding what is good or not good, to boast of it is called arrogance (*jing*). Whenever Lord Wenzhong...
It is regrettable that an impartial mind is so difficult to attain; could it truly be as such?
There was a monk from the Tang dynasty named Yuanxiao, a native of Haedong (Korea). Having first traveled by sea, he set out to seek the Way at famous mountains.

Walking alone across a desolate marsh, he stayed overnight among the graves. Being extremely thirsty, he reached out his hand to cup water from a hollow; there he found a spring, sweet and cool. At dawn—

He looked at it closely; it was a skull. He loathed it intensely and felt as though he wanted to vomit it away. Suddenly, he had a profound realization and sighed, saying: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, the skull is no different [from my own nature]. The Great Teacher Tathāgata said, 'The three realms are but mind. How could he have deceived me?
Thereupon, he no longer sought a teacher and returned to the East Sea that very day, where he composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Great...

To propagate the teachings of the Great, Perfect, and Sudden [Vehicle]. Upon reading his biography up to this point, I recalled the story from the Jin dynasty of Yue Guang and the snake in the wine cup, and composed a verse:
"The skulls in the night grave were originally but water; The bow-shadow in the guest’s cup was never a snake.
Within this, there is no place for birth or extinction; Laughing, I grasp the remaining scrolls as the incense smoke slants."
The Great Being Zao Bo and National Teacher Qingliang both propagated the Mahāyāna sūtras and composed commentaries and treatises that became the preeminent traditions throughout the land.

Nevertheless, the conduct of these two masters was entirely different. Zao Bo walked barefoot without impediment, moving with transcendent ease and spontaneity, embodying a mind of non-obstruction in all phenomena (*sarva-vastu-asaṅga*).
Qingliang, however, was refined and upright as a jade pillar; he feared the five colors and the filth of the world, regulating himself according to his ten vows.
As for the person [who made this assessment], many praise Zao Bo for his carefree and unrestrained manner, while laughing at Qing Liang’s constraints.

In my view, this is not what is appropriate for the Huayan school. I said: "This is most certainly not so. Had Zao Bo shaved his head and become a bhikṣu, he would likely have practiced in no way different from Qing Liang.
This is because this sutra takes whatever conditions it encounters as its fundamental principle of harmony; it is not like other sutras which..."
This is a matter of scale.
During the Jin dynasty, Kumārajīva followed his mother to Kucha as a child. He carried the Buddha’s almsbowl upon his head and thought to himself, "The shape of this bowl is very large;
why is it so light? Immediately, it became heavy, and he let it drop with a cry. His mother asked him the reason, and he replied, "It was my mind [that made it so]."
There is discrimination; thus, the alms bowls have lightness and heaviness. By this I know that all phenomena arrive according to thought.

When thought has not yet arisen, their measure is equal to the great void. Yet, why is it that the spiritual efficacy of those who currently engage in active discrimination is not uniform, as the myriad categories appear in chaotic profusion?
It is said: these are all disordered thoughts and false imaginings, like events in a troubled dream.
This is because their mental power is dim and their faculties are inferior. Alas! There is no human being who does not possess a heart of loyalty and filial piety.
Yet when Wang Xiang lay upon the ice, the fish leaped up; when Geng Gong prayed for the well, the spring became clear and cold. Why is this?
It is because they cultivated these virtues with single-minded devotion; thus, the spiritual efficacy responded as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound.
When Bodhidharma first traveled from the Liang to the Wei dynasties, he journeyed beneath Mount Song and leaned his staff against Shaolin, sitting in meditation facing a wall.
This was not, however, the practice of *dhyāna*. For a long time, no one could fathom his purpose, and consequently, they came to regard Bodhidharma as a practitioner of *dhyāna*.
Now, *dhyāna* (meditation) is merely one among the various forms of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*); how could it suffice to encompass the entirety of a sage? And yet—
Those of that time who compiled the histories further included him among the ranks of those who practice dhyāna, placing him in the company of those like withered wood or extinguished ashes.
Nevertheless, the Sage does not stop at dhyāna, yet he does not deviate from dhyāna;
just as the *I Ching* emerges from yin and yang, yet does not deviate from yin and yang.
According to an old account, the Fourth Patriarch, the Great Master, resided at Mount Pòtóu. On that mountain there was an anonymous old monk who planted nothing but pines;
people called him the "Pine-Planting Wayfarer. Once, he requested of the Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied:
"You are already old; even if you were to hear [the Dharma], would you be able to transform others extensively? If you could come again, I might still wait for you. Thereupon, he departed.
Walking by the water's edge, he saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman said, "I have father and brothers; you may go seek them.
He replied, "If they grant me permission, I shall venture to do so. The woman nodded her head in agreement, and the old monk turned his staff and returned.
She departed. The girl was the younger daughter of the Zhou clan. As soon as she married, she became pregnant; her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere to go, she spent her days spinning for hire in the village and stayed at night beneath a public hostel. She subsequently gave birth to a son, whom she deemed an ill omen and threw into the water.
The next day, she saw him swimming upstream against the current, his physical form radiant and clear. She was greatly astonished and finally took him up.
When he reached the age of a young adult, he followed his mother to beg for food. The villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname.
The Fourth Patriarch saw him on the road at Huangmei and asked him playfully, "What is your surname? He replied, "I certainly have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.

The Patriarch asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch said, "Then you have no surname? He replied, "Because its nature is emptiness, it has none. The Patriarch then transformed him.

The mother sent [her son] forth into the monastic life when he was seven years old. The various lodgings have now become a monastery called Fomu (Buddha-Mother). The Zhou clan is particularly prominent there.
Looking out from Mount Pòtóu, the physical remains of the Master [Huineng] still exist. At Dongchan Monastery in Huangmei, there is the tomb of Fomu; the people have erected a stupa over it.

from night until dawn it was as if it were day. A wondrous fragrance permeated the people. The entire family was filled with wonder and alarm.

Who could have known that he would later dwell in a public lodging and be born into a common household? Furthermore, it says: His father doted on him and consequently ordered him to recite [the scriptures]."
The Book [of History] does not know from where it obtained these words; its narratives are as wildly extravagant as this, for the most part.

He spoke of this to him. Duanji stuck out his tongue in great astonishment. They had been companions for a very long time; it was only in his later years that he moved to Bai Zhang Mountain in Xinwu.

Examining the timing, the old woman had died long ago; thus, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* (Dà Sòng gāo sēng zhuàn), which claims that the old woman told Duanji to go see Bai Zhang, is incorrect.
Master Yunju Foyin said: "Master Yunmen’s preaching of the Dharma was like clouds; he absolutely did not like people recording his words.

"You may flee, but there is no way to avoid the fire. When the fire arrived, it was extinguished. Venerable Yan-yang lived alone on the mountain;
snakes and tigers would come into his hands to be eaten. Master Gui-zong Chang was mowing grass when he saw a snake and cut it down.
A nearby monk said, "I have long heard of Gui-zong; today I finally see a monk of coarse conduct. Chang said, "Are you coarse, or am I coarse? I have heard that one who is close..."

There are four ways to verify the mind in proximity to Prajñā: namely, verification through phenomena (*shi*), verification through principle (*li*), entry into both phenomena and principle (*ru-jushi*), and emergence from both phenomena and principle (*chu-jushi*).

Beyond phenomena and principle, the Chan school further possesses the application of the "concealed point" (*zangfeng*) in four ways: using it to cultivate oneself through close proximity, and using the application of the concealed point to transform others.

While the forms themselves differ, the jewel undergoes no change. For example, when the jewel manifests blackness, a person might take the jewel itself to be black."

It is not seeing the pearl. To seek the pearl apart from the black is also not seeing the pearl. To take the brightness and the blackness together as being non-existent as the pearl is also not seeing the pearl.
Mazu’s teaching of the Dharma—immediately taking the delusion to be the truth—is just like taking the black to be the pearl.

Shenxiu’s teaching of the Dharma, which requires the exhaustion of delusions before one can see the enlightened nature, is just like seeking the truth apart from delusion. It is just like [seeking the pearl] apart from the black.
The black one seeks the pearl; the ox-head speaks the Dharma. All is like a dream; originally there is no affair. Both truth and falsehood are non-existent.
It is just as when both light and dark are entirely absent, leaving nothing to be called a pearl.

Illumination follows along with the murky obscurity; wherever it extends, there is no illumination. It is most subtle and most wondrous; it knows that dharmas are without knowing. This "knowing through non-knowing" is the essential point.

How can one know that Master Xiu was not a hidden means?

Tang Monk Fuli possessed a profound understanding of the Dharma. His contemporaries held him in the highest esteem. He composed a verse on Reality and Delusion (*zhenwang*) and addressed it to scholars throughout the land, saying:
"The nature of reality is fundamentally pure; from where does deluded thought arise? If delusion is born from reality, where can this delusion cease?
If there is no beginning, then there is no end; if there were an end, there must have been a beginning. Without beginning and without end, it is eternal."

I harbor confusion regarding this principle; I pray that you will elucidate its profound mystery and analyze how one transcends birth and death. Master Qingliang replied: "When deluded regarding the truth, false thoughts arise;
when awakened to the truth, false thoughts cease immediately. That which is capable of delusion is not itself the object of delusion; how could they remain similar for long?"
From the very beginning, one has never awakened; therefore, it is said that delusion is beginningless. To know that delusion is inherently true is precisely the eternally wondrous principle.
If the discriminating mind is not yet forgotten, by what means can one transcend birth and death? Master Guifeng replied: "The fundamental nature is pure, yet fundamentally lacks awareness;
from this, deluded thoughts arise. When one knows that both truth and delusion are empty, and when one knows that emptiness causes delusion to cease, this state of cessation is called 'existence'."
End. When deluded, it is called "beginningless. Causes and conditions are like illusions and dreams; what end can there be, and what beginning? This is the source of all sentient beings;
by exhausting it, one emerges from birth and death. It is also said: Many people claim that the Real gives rise to the false, and therefore the false is never exhausted.
To resolve this principle, he again answers the previous verse, saying: "It is not that the real gives rise to the delusory; rather, the delusory arises from being deluded regarding the real.

When one awakens to the fact that the delusory is fundamentally the real, knowing the real, the delusory ceases. The cessation of the delusory seems like an end, while awakening seems like a beginning. Yet the nature of both delusion and awakening is empty;
being empty, they have neither end nor beginning. Birth and death arise from this delusion; by penetrating this, one transcends birth and death."—I.
I tasted the words of the two elders’ responses; neither fully accorded with the intent of Fu Li’s question.
He asked how deluded thoughts arise when the true Dharma is fundamentally pure, yet they merely said, "One is deluded and fails to realize it.

Who could not have answered that? Therefore, I shall clarify their meaning by composing this verse: The true Dharma is fundamentally without self-nature; It arises as defiled or pure according to conditions. Failing to understand this is called ignorance.
Clarity is itself Buddha-wisdom; ignorance is entirely deluded sentiment, while awareness is entirely true principle. In this single thought-moment, one transcends past and present;
where could one seek its beginning or end? It is fundamentally beyond verbal expression; conceptual discrimination is birth and death.
Master Yúnnán once said: "The Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to comprehend. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should preach by means of skillful expedients according to what they can understand.
One should not crave fame, profit, or honor, but should only contemplate benefiting oneself and others, dedicating [the merit] toward Bodhi. This is for the sake of propagating the Dharma.
This is what Jùn spoke of. The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* states:

"Sentient beings of the final age who wish to practice cultivation should, throughout their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). When those spiritual teachers wish to come near them, they should sever all anger and resentment."
"Manifesting conditions of both adversity and favor, like empty space" refers to those who seek the Way but lack diligent application.
Nevertheless, if disciples are able not to forget their diligence, then the teacher will not find it too harsh to be overly strict.
At present, students have not yet fully perfected the rites of respectful homage; to demand of them that they withhold the Dharma would be an error. Attendant.
Jin said, "If that is so, may I hear the manner in which the Tathāgatas of the three periods bestow the gift of Dharma? He replied, "The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

When Chan Master Daguanying first set out from Eastern Wu, he was only sixteen or seventeen years old. While mooring his boat at the Qinhuai River, he stayed overnight at Fengxian Temple.

they have no secret treasury. It is like a wooden puppet operated by a magician: although people see it bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up, no one knows what is within that causes it to act thus.
The Buddha-dharma is not like this; it causes all sentient beings to fully know and see. How so?
It should be said that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a secret treasury. The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is as you have said;
the Tathāgata truly has no secret treasury. Why is this?
Just as the full autumn moon, situated in the sky, is manifest, pure, and free from obscuration so that all people may behold it, the words of the Tathāgata are likewise; they reveal [the truth]."

It is revealed and made manifest, pure and free from obscuration. The ignorant do not understand it and call it a "secret treasury," but the wise, having fully realized it, do not designate it as a treasury.

if one carefully savors the meaning of Master Mì’s words, one can let out a laugh that will resound for a thousand years.

'To give rise to the mind' means to manifest the One Mind through all phenomena. If one gives rise to the mind while dwelling [on something], then..."
"Subhūti, if one dwells in a mind of evil arising, then evil manifests and the original mind is obscured. If there is no dwelling, the worlds of the ten directions are but a single mind.

Daily affairs obscure the person of original nature.
A monk asked Elder Huitang, "The Fifth Patriarch’s predecessor, the Pine-Planting Wayfarer, was once born through the medium of a Zhou family woman.
Since those three conditions were not in harmony, from what did he arise? The Elder smiled and said, "Have you heard..."
"Jyotiṣka was born from within fire; Yi Yin was born from the hollow of a mulberry tree. He replied, "I have heard this.
You do not doubt that those two were born without the three conditions, yet you alone doubt the Five Patriarchs?

Nowadays, among the scholar-officials who take an interest in the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the lineage), all harbor such doubts. Upon hearing these words, there is none who does not [realize the truth]."

I am relieved. I believe that what the old man showed was not intended to exhaustively reveal the fundamental meaning of the Buddhist vehicle (*yāna*), but rather to settle the wild emotions of his disciples according to their specific capacities.
As the Great Master Mazu said: "The Buddha is the Capable One (*Śakya-muni*).

He possesses wisdom, is skillful in responding to circumstances, and can shatter the net of doubts of all sentient beings, enabling them to escape the bonds of existence and non-existence. Is this not precisely what he meant?
The *Zongjing lu* states: "Although mind is itself karma and karma is itself mind, since [karma] arises from the mind, one must likewise experience its results from the mind.
How, then, can one eliminate the retribution of these deluded karmas in the present? It answers: "Simply by realizing non-action (*wu zuo*), karma naturally becomes empty. Therefore it is said:
'If one realizes the non-existence of evil karma, one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime. Furthermore, it says: 'Although there is the performance of karma...'"

If one realizes that the mind does not grasp at objects, then objects will not arise of their own accord.
When no phenomena can entice the emotions, how could karma be formed? I have once composed a verse to explain this principle: Raising the hand...

Birth and death, the thunder that grows the plantain tree, and the iron that turns toward the magnet—none of these have a creator, yet they possess such power.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Entering the inconceivable realm. This is like borrowing a seat from King Dīpaṃkara, taking food and fragrant soil, and condensing the vastness of kalpas into a single day so that their relative sizes may coexist;
thus one can spiritually realize the wondrous intent. As for the statement regarding all śrāvakas:
Upon hearing this Dharma-door of the inconceivable liberation, all should weep aloud, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.

It is extremely difficult to understand and penetrate. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* states: "When one person gives rise to true realization and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely extinguished.

This is truly the wondrously enlightened essence of clarity. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

The junior monk said, "Elder brother, why have you come to such an extreme? Huanglong rebuked him, saying, "You vulgar fellow! Truly, he did not realize he was bowing to him.
His immovability was like that of a mountain, as exemplified by this.

This leads to its widespread dissemination and the extinction of our school. In the age of the Dharma’s decline, people mostly possess only dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

Because Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended conceptualization, one knows that liberation from birth and death occurs within a single phrase.

Master Longya had a half-length portrait painted of himself; his disciple Baoci Kuanghua composed a eulogy for it, saying: "The sun rises over the connected mountains;
the moon is full facing the door. It is not that he has no body; it is simply that he does not wish to reveal it entirely. These two elders were the realized ones of Dongshan.

a shake of the bell causes the nine heavens to return to their source. In the midst of the correct, the subtle embrace interpenetrates and reverses; should one hesitate, the sharp edge loses its majesty.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "As I have taught the Dharma, it is like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not Dharma.
Among the sages and worthies who have commented upon this in India and here in China, numbering no fewer than a thousand, none has grasped the Buddha’s intent as well as Asaṅga.

like a raft moving upon water, it does not truly abide. "Non-Dharma" refers to the two extremes. If even a raft is not identical [to its user], how much less could one abide within the two extremes?
Therefore it is said: "How much more so regarding non-Dharma. A Great Being’s verse says: "To cross the river, one must..."
