Thus, the fundamental tenets of the Cao-Dong school contain the expression that "the mixed cannot be made uniform," meaning that categories are not to be equated.
When Chan Master Yunfeng Yue traveled again to Letan, he met Chan Master Nan once more. They recounted their parting and reminisced about the past, finding great joy in each other’s company.
After some time, he was further urged to visit the elder Shishuang Ciming. Upon arriving at Shishuang, he stayed at a manor house before the mountain;
hearing of the master’s straightforward and unpretentious character, he regretted his coming and did not enter the gate, instead proceeding directly to Nanyue.

Before a month had passed at Fuyan, he served as the head of the Secretariat (Chamberlain for Records). Suddenly, the Elder Master Xian passed away, and the Prefectural Governor invited Ciming to reside there.

Upon first hearing the night discourse, in which [Ciming] disparaged the divergent interpretations of various schools—interpretations that [the Prefect] himself had acquired through years of arduous effort—he was filled with admiration and immediately offered his sincere devotion to inquire about the Way.
He went three times, each time being met with insults and driven away; unable to restrain his indignation, he departed.
Having returned home, he went back the following day. Ciming scolded him as before. He then said, "I came solely because I did not understand;

a *kalyāṇamitra* ought to employ skillful means. To receive nothing but scolding without being granted instruction—could this truly be the manner of transmitting the Dharma since the time of the ancestors?
Ciming was startled and said, "Monk Nan, I thought you were..."
This person—did he take it as a riddle of abuse? When Huanglong heard these words, it was as if the bottom of his bucket had fallen out; he rose from his prostrations with sweat pouring down.
He then composedly discussed the *nidāna* of Zhaozhou and presented this verse: "Standing out from the forest is Zhaozhou; The old woman’s discernment leaves no room for cause.
Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; Travelers, do not make the road your enemy. Ciming.
Upon reading it, he laughed and said, "The verse is excellent, but I would change one word. He said: "An old woman’s realization has its source.
His wit and subtlety were once again like this. Huanglong took his leave and asked, "Ultimately, what is the Great Matter?
Ciming rebuked him, saying, "Putting on clothes and eating food is not the ultimate; defecating and urinating is not the ultimate. I...
Once, while traveling to Fuyan, I surveyed the magnificent topography of its mountains and rivers and read what Dazhu Huihai had recorded:
"This mountain increases one's willpower; those who dwell here often attain the Way. Thus, when our ancestors transmitted the Dharma, none did so without relying on it.
Although the flourishing of the Great Dharma must depend upon people, it was here that Mazu received the seal of certification from Master Xiang. Its Way—
He was greatly renowned in Jiangxi. Now, the deeds of Ciming and Huanglong are again similar; this too is truly remarkable. Master Sheng said:
"Striking the air produces sound; striking wood makes no sound. Once, when Chan Master Fayan suddenly heard the sound of the vegetarian bell, he asked his attendant, "Do you hear it?
If you heard it just now, you do not hear it now. If you hear it now," [you did not hear it just now].
"You did not hear it just now. Do you understand?
A monk who had once ascended the third storey of the treasury took up a staff that Sengzhao (Sida) had carried throughout his life and set it upright.
Doubts and hesitations arose in abundance, and he could not settle his mind. Suddenly, he thought to himself: "I must let go of everything. He then raised the staff and placed it down.
The walking staff stood upright and did not lean. I asked him what the reason for this was. He replied, "It is not only with a walking staff that this is so.
In all matters, if there is a deliberate intention (*citta*), error will inevitably arise. Observe, for instance, when children cut paper: if they apply a deliberate intention, they fail;
if they do not apply a deliberate intention, they proceed directly without difficulty. Therefore, a practitioner of the Way must never for a moment forget *pratyavekṣaṇā* (contemplative awareness)."
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "You originally do not know that all these floating, mundane, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise right where they are and perish right where they are.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "For example, a fierce fire cannot burn the fuel; it is called 'burning the fuel' when the fire has emerged and the wood is exhausted.
The *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* says: "The principle regarding the sense organs and their objects is likewise; why should the wise be startled or find it strange? —The Zen monk.
Only when one has attained such thorough insight into this can one enter the Dharma-gate of the letter *A*.
Kang Senghui was a man from India who first arrived at Jianye in the tenth year of the Chiku era of the Wu dynasty. He constructed a thatched hut, established an image, and practiced the Way.
Sun Quan, suspecting him of practicing eccentricity, summoned him and asked, "What spiritual manifestations do you possess? He replied, "The Tathāgata..."
Since his traces were transferred [to this world], more than a thousand years have suddenly passed. His remaining bones and *śarīra* relics possess a divine radiance that is boundless.

In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stupas; the rise of such pagodas and monasteries manifests his enduring transformation. Zhiquan said, "If you obtain the *śarīra*, I shall commission the construction of a stupa for it;
if it proves to be false, the state shall impose its standard punishment. He requested a period of seven days and then addressed his subordinates.

They collectively consecrated a pure chamber, placing a copper bottle atop a tile, burning incense, and making offerings with prayers. When the appointed time arrived, there was no response. They continued their efforts for three weeks;
suddenly, they heard a sharp metallic sound from within the bottle. Indeed, they obtained śarīra (relics) to show to Sun Quan. Quan, together with his ministers, gathered to observe them;

the relics appeared in five colors, each corresponding to one of the five elements. Sun Quan rose in great astonishment and said, "This is a rare and auspicious omen! Thus it is recorded in the *Shi* (History).
Tandi’s father was Rong, who once served as the Vice-Governor of Jizhou.

His mother, Lady Huang, while napping during the day, dreamed that a monk called out to her as "Mother," entrusting her with a fly-whisk (*zhuchi*) and two iron-inlaid book-weights. Upon waking, both objects were still there;
she subsequently conceived and gave birth to Di. These two items were the possessions of Tandi’s previous incarnation, Dharma Master Hongjue, who had served under Yao Chang.
This was offered during the lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Tracing back the life of the Great Awakened One (Hóngjué), it coincided precisely with the day he entrusted these items.

Because of the height of his sincerity, he was able to bring forth śarīra while alive; because of the power of his profound vows, he was likewise able to carry his long-held possessions with him at death.

Alas! If the power of a sincere and great vow can still reverse the cycle of birth and death and bring about mastery according to one's will, how much more so for those who guard the city of the mind?
Zhuangzi said: "To hide a boat in a ravine; to hide a mountain in a marsh.

Commentators have explained these words as they flow along, yet when it comes to the statement, "To hide the world under heaven within the world," there is none who does not sit down abruptly in a state of trepidation, setting aside their brush to contemplate it.
When the Elder Huìtáng once asked his students what the meaning of this was, many responded; Huìtáng laughed and said, "You are all skilled at explaining it."
This is the principle. I have composed a verse to record its meaning: "The mind of the world knows that nothing can be hidden; In confusion they sniff the tracks and seek only the fragrance.
Only when one can truly take a step from the top of a hundred-foot pole Does one first see the horned sheep hanging from the treetop. He asked again:
"When Liezi encountered two children debating whether the sun was near or far and could not resolve it, he questioned Confucius about it. Confucius did not answer."
"What was his intention? The scholars all said, "Even a sage such as our Master could not discern this principle;
therefore, he remained silent. Huìtáng also laughed at them. I composed a verse to explain it: "Cold and heat, far and near—doubts increase ever more.
He did not answer, for it was like piercing the very point of pain. Yet they still pursue it like children, their quarreling never ending; How could Zhòngní alone be ancient?"
It is difficult to know.
Formerly, when the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang was serving as an official in Luoyang, he once traveled to Mount Song. He dismissed his attendants and went forth with unrestrained ease.
Upon reaching a mountain temple, he entered its gate; there, tall bamboos filled the courtyard, the frost was clear, birds were singing, and the scenery was vivid and bright.
Wenzhong was resting at the palace steps when an elderly monk nearby was reading a sutra with unperturbed composure. When Wenzhong spoke to him, the monk did not look back or respond much.
Wenzhong found this strange and asked, "How long has it been since you have lived in the mountains? He replied, "For a very long time.

Wenzhong further asked, "What sutra are you reciting? He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. Wenzhong said, "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, when they faced the moment of death, they were for the most part..."

As they were conversing and laughing, [the monk] passed away. Wen Zhong asked, "By what path did he attain this? The monk replied, "It was simply through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*.
Wen Zhong asked again, "Now, why is it that you are so silent and devoid of such qualities? The old monk smiled and said, "The ancients maintained concentration and wisdom in every thought-moment;

how could they be disturbed at the moment of death? The people of today maintain distraction in every thought-moment; how could they achieve stability at the moment of death? Wen Zhong was greatly astonished.
He was aware of his own knees bending. Xie Hishen once composed a literary record of these matters, stating that Fahua’s physical appearance was extraordinary and ancient;

he gazed straight ahead without blinking, often speaking and laughing alone, frequently walking through the marketplaces, running with his robes hitched up, or sometimes pointing his finger at the sky and standing still for a long time.
He associated with butchers and wine-sellers, eating and drinking without restraint.

Zhe was commonly regarded by both monastics and laypeople as a "mad monk. When Master Huai had not yet left the household life, the Master saw him and patted his back, saying, "You will become Deshan or Linji.
When Prime Minister Lü Xǔgōng asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, he replied, "Originally there is not a single thing;
in a single flavor, all is truly real. When a monk asked, "Does the world have a Buddha? he replied, "Mañjuśrī is in the temple."
Someone asked, "Are you a commoner or a sage? He raised his hand and said, "I do not dwell here; I am about to manifest my transformation.

He then composed a final verse, the meaning of which was inscrutable. Afterward, he said, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have perfected the Jetavana land and manifested my body to propagate the teaching.
Now I return to the South. Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully on his right side. (Qingli Wuyin)
The "Son" refers to the twenty-third day of the eleventh month.

During the Yuanfeng era, Chan Master Zhaojue transformed the East Lin monastery from a Vinaya residence into a *conglin* (monastic community). Monastics from all over the world gathered there at his reputation;
they all held him in faith, reverence, and awe, regarding him as a Mahāsattva in flesh and bone. Among those who were recognized and favored by him...
He will surely become renowned in all directions; yet he has never bestowed [the Dharma] lightly upon others. Chan Master Xiaonan of Luohan Temple was a successor of Master You of Yunju;
his insight into the Way was clear and lucid, yet it remained unknown to the world. Once, when he arrived at Donglin, Zhaojue struck the bell to assemble the congregation.
He went out to welcome him upon the Qingxi Brook. His disciples were greatly astonished. From that time on, Nan’s fame grew increasingly prominent.
Chan Master Foyin returned once more to Yunju. Elder Lingyuan initially came from Longshan and lived among the community.

He had long concealed himself in obscurity. When Foyin ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, he requested him to serve as the head of the community (*zuòyuán*). The ceremonial protocols for this were exceptionally distinguished.
Lingyuan accepted the position, and those studying in the monastic groves (*cónglín*) drew closer to him daily; thus they came to know that the legacy of the Elder Huítáng truly endured.
Alas! The way in which the former sages perfected those who were vessels of the Dharma, thereby increasing its weight in the world, was precisely like this.
Yao was not incapable of executing the Four Villains; rather, he raised the Sixteen Sons, leaving them behind to await Shun.
Even the deeds of the ancient sages could not transcend this principle. Did the Two Elders also understand this?
It has been nearly a hundred years since the ancient Abbot [Zhaozhou] departed from the era of Yunmen, yet he is still called his successor.
Qing Huayan had never even met Dayang; he accepted him as his successor without hesitation solely because of the words of Fushan Yuan.

Both of these elders were such that they remained self-possessed in the transmission of words and deeds; they held themselves in high regard, yet regarded the Dharma with great lightness. As for the ancients...
Those who held the Dharma in high esteem were Yongjia and Huangbo.

Yongjia, upon reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, awakened to the essence of the Buddha-mind and went to see the Sixth Patriarch, saying, "I wish to establish the definitive teaching. Huangbo awakened to the intent of Mazu and became the successor of Baizhang;
thus, Baizhang sighed that he could not surpass him.

Zen Master Dizang Chen was one who was able to greatly revitalize the teachings of Xuefeng and Xuansha. Was this not the result of his profound secrecy regarding the Great Dharma and his practice of tranquil withdrawal?
I have often imagined what he was like as a person: at an ancient temple on the outskirts of a city, the gate appeared as cold as dead ashes.
His countenance was serene and deep; he would jest with visiting Zen practitioners, saying, "The various quarters speak of Zen with such clamor—how can it compare [to this]?"
"In this world of mine, I plow the fields to earn my food; how profound this is!
When I first resided at Mount Huanglong, I composed the 'Twelve Hours of the Day' verse for Zen practitioners, saying:
My livelihood has nothing to behold; Day after day, it grows ever the same. At the hour of the Rat (midnight), weary as if dead, I am bitten by lice; I move my toes."
At the hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.), when the rooster crows, the gruel-bowl fish bell howls; in haste, one ties the skirt and searches for the laces of the socks.

At the hour of Yin (3–5 a.m.), at the break of dawn, one suddenly yawns and stretches; the ridges of the two eyebrows weigh as much as a thousand catties. At the hour of Mao (5–7 a.m.), when the sun rises, one stirs up a fuss within oneself; the eyes recite the sutras while the mouth twists in contradiction.

At the hour of Chen (7–9 a.m.), saliva flows from the teeth; the belly is emptied, yet the lips are left wanting. At the hour of Si (9–11 a.m.), regarding the matters before one’s eyes, though seen with clarity, they cannot be described as they truly are.

At noon, the sun is at its zenith; my robes are mended by myself. Suddenly, I thread the needle, and my entire body is revealed. At the hour of *di*, before the sun has set, I finally break my sleep; I wash my face and feel about my nose.
At the hour of *shen*, the hour of *pu*, one is most true to one's original nature: things go smoothly and one is joyful, while things go against one and one is angry.

When the sun sets at the hour of *you*, the mouth hangs upon the wall and the mirror is empty. At midday, the dipper is centered; at the hour of *xu*, dusk falls, and activity becomes subtle. As the eyes open and close, the crows caw "wu-cu-li."
At the hour of Ren-ding (Hai), when one speaks, there is immediate understanding. The Dharma-body sleeps without a blanket or cover. Sitting, they form a thicket; walking, they form a troop.

They move with lively agility, free from all obstructions. Should you so much as touch them, it is like striking bare flesh with moxa. Originally, there is not a single thing to be managed or performed.
Everyone gathers together to eat stalks of vegetables.
When Chan Master Yunfeng Yue first arrived at Dayu in Gao’an, he met Master Zhi.
Zhi asked him, "What do you seek by coming here? Yue replied, "I intend to study the Buddha-dharma. Zhi said, "How can the Buddha-dharma be studied lightly?

While your physical strength is robust, go on one round of begging alms for the assembly; it will not be too late to study then. Yue was of pure and sincere disposition, and he accepted his words with faith.
Having spoken thus, he immediately went out to beg for alms. Upon his return, Zhì moved his residence to Cuìyán. Huìyè again visited Zhì’s location, seeking to enter the inner circle of disciples.
Zhì said, "Set aside the Buddha-dharma for a moment; the assembly is cold at night and requires charcoal. You must go begging for charcoal once more."

"It is never too late to study. Huiyue then went out to beg for alms again. At the end of the year, he returned carrying charcoal and requested further instruction. Sengzhi said, "The Buddha-dharma does not fear being ruined.

The position of *karmadāna* (venerable administrator) is currently vacant; you should take up this office and not decline it. He then struck the *gaṇḍī* bell to inform the assembly and formally requested him for the post.
Huiyue showed a look of reluctance; as he rose from his prostrations, he felt regret and wished to abandon his post. However, since he had already undertaken the responsibility, he remained.

He took a rest there. However, he regretted not understanding what Master Zhi’s intention truly was. One day, while binding a broken bucket with bamboo strips, the strips struck a basin and caused it to fall to the ground.
At that moment, he attained great enlightenment and finally saw the point of Master Zhi’s application. He ran to see Zhi, who called out to him with a smile, "Venerable Karmadāna, congratulations!
You have finished the Great Matter. Before Yue could utter a single word, he prostrated himself twice, his sweat falling like rain.
He departed; thus, his school’s tradition was solitary and austere, and never once did anyone attempt to emulate it.
Master Nan once said to the elder Yuan of Danning, "If he wishes for everyone to attain such realization, how could that ever be possible?"

Chan Master Shending Yin, during his youth, traveled with several senior monks to Mount Nanyue. One monk was discussing the vehicle of the patriarchal lineage (zongcheng) with great erudition and eloquence.
As they happened upon a mountain inn where wild rice was being prepared for a meal, the monk continued his discourse without ceasing. Shending said:
The Master said, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Consciousness-only is mind-only. 'Eye-sound, ear-form'—whose words are these?
The monk replied, "They are verses by the Great Master Fayan. Yunyan asked, "What is their meaning?

He replied, "Because it is mind-only, the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another. Because it is consciousness-only, sounds and forms are vividly manifest. Yunyan said, "Tongue and taste are the sense organ..."

"Is it so? he asked. Yuanzhen replied, "It is. Yuanzhen then used his chopsticks to pick up some vegetables and put them in his mouth; with his words muffled by the food, he said, "What do you mean by 'mutual entry'?
Those present looked at one another in great astonishment, none able to offer a reply. Yuanzhen said, "The pleasures of the road do not mean you have reached home.
To see and understand down to the subtle is not called seeing the Way. You must investigate authentically; you must awaken authentically. Otherwise, you will end up before King Yama."
Great King, do not fear prolixity.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* reveals the practice of the Bodhisattva through the perfect realization of the two awakenings. First, Wonhyo composed a commentary on it.

He realized that [the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*] takes the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial—as its central tenet; thus, it depicts Śākyamuni sitting on an ox-cart with a desk placed between its two horns, relying upon a "grass-text" (a draft).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* takes the realization that all beings possess the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) as its central tenet;

therefore, the introductory narrative of the sutra does not specify the time or location. Furthermore, when examining the era of its translation, the historical records likewise do not mention it. (Xiao)
The public exposition of the Dharma-tables is the Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) in profound accord with the Buddha’s intent; is it not the reflection of the spirit of self-awakened mind?
When the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, was in his period of concealment, he lived among the common people, mingling with laborers, merchants, and farmers for sixteen years.
During that time, even barbarian children, fishermen, peddlers, and kitchen wives were able to call out to him.

As for you, your virtue was bestowed upon others and your Way gained the trust of the world. Although successive emperors could not serve or befriend you as their teacher, this was because your conduct accorded with the standard of the sages and worthies;
thus, no one perceived any distinction between noble and base. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* states:
"The Emperor summoned him repeatedly, but the Master ultimately did not go. He said, 'My appearance is not prominent. If a person from the North were to see me...'"
This must be a disparagement of the Dharma; can this truly be the word of the Patriarchs? It is the speech of those lacking benevolence.

How could the Perfected One ever have been concerned with the physical body? All the more so for one whose celestial form and countenance embody the Way, who gathers all beings through compassion—how could such a person fail to have confidence in themselves?

The Master Shitou had lived in a hermitage on Mount Nantai for many years. One day, he happened to see someone carrying rice up the mountain and asked him why. The man replied, "I am delivering rice as an offering.

The following day, the Master immediately moved his hermitage to the end of a ridge beam and eventually passed away there; a stupa remains at that site. Baizhang Monastery is located at the very summit. Every day, the Master would perform manual labor to repay the offerings provided to him.

When someone urged him to stop, he replied: "If I do not work, who will provide the food? If I do not eat, how can I preach the Dharma? If I do not preach the Dharma, how can I save sentient beings? If I do not save sentient beings, how can I repay my debt of gratitude? Thus, he continued his labors until the end.
It was said: "I have no virtue to weary others. The multitude could not bear it and hid away his tools; consequently, he did not eat.
Thus arose the saying, "One day without work, one day without food. The former masters of our tradition mostly acted in this manner throughout their lives:

for instance, the Sixth Patriarch used stones as a waist-weight, and Niu-t'ou carried grain on his back to provide for the community. Now, young bhikṣus hold up their alms bowls with furrowed brows and say: [This is not the way.]
"My arms ache.

This refers to Chan Master Xuedou’s *Zuǎngīng Sònggǔ* (Verses on Ancient Cases by the Patriarchs). In its opening verse, concerning the First Patriarch’s failure to find resonance with Emperor Wu of Liang, he writes:

"The whole nation pursues him, yet he does not return; for ten thousand autumns and ten thousand springs, he is remembered in vain. This is a profound lament that Old Xiao failed [to grasp the truth].

This is a passage from the *Yuci* (遇詞). Those who are ignorant have recorded the following account at the beginning: "After Bodhidharma had departed, Master Zhigong asked, 'Does Your Majesty recognize this man?
He is but an emanation-body of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who has come to this land to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal.
Why do you not pay him homage? Old Xiao wished to pursue him, but Zhigong said, 'Even if the entire nation were to...'"

People pursue it, yet it does not come back again. How could Xuedou not have known that Master Zhi passed away in the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era, while Bodhidharma arrived in Jinling in the first year of the Putong era?
By this, I know that the one who composed this narrative did not intend it to be Xuedou’s own view.
Furthermore, in current transcriptions, it is written as "Gai Guo," which is all the more laughable. Moreover, [he] composed a verse on Dongshan’s "Three Hemp Plants."
Jin said: "One can recall how Master Lu of Changqing understood the principle of 'when it is appropriate to weep and when it is not. He employed the words of Changqing;
upon hearing Master Lu’s remark, Changqing wept and then asked the assembly, 'Tell me, is it appropriate to weep or not?
This account appears in the *Chuan Deng Lu*. Yet those who are ignorant easily say, 'It is appropriate to laugh, not to weep,' thereby missing the essential point."
How lamentable! When Lord Wang Wen Gong encountered many Chan practitioners who spoke of their encounters with Han Tuozhi and Da Dian, they often addressed him with reckless talk.
Lord Wang sighed in regret that these Chan practitioners frequently spoke from mere conjecture without inquiring into the underlying principles;

for this reason, those who slander them are numerous. Therefore, those who are dedicated to the religious teachings should investigate and verify these matters; they must not be treated with casual indifference.
A monk asked me, "Regarding the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms, have there been many masters of the ancestral school who have explained their meaning?
I replied, "There is a verse by Caoxi [Huineng] that explains it in detail, which says: 'The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in the mind.
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six..."

The seven fruits and causes undergo transformation; they merely change their names while lacking any substantial nature. If one leaves no lingering attachment toward that which undergoes transformation, then amidst all proliferation, one eternally abides in the *nāga-samādhi*.

Because the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness take the direct objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their object, it is said: "The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror.
These all undergo transformation at the level of the fruit. Since the sixth and seventh consciousnesses have no separate substance, they are only able to cognize [their objects].
This is the equality of nature; all these are transformations within the causal state.
Ying of Shaowu possessed a disposition of expansive clarity and luminous salvation; he was truly a "fang-toothed" disciple of the ancestral school.

He once stayed as a guest at Yunju, where he shut his room and did not interact with others. Looking down upon the four seas, he found no one whose views accorded with his own, and he said: "I shall..."
He passed away on this mountain. One night, while reading the *Ten Clarifications* (*Shiming lun*) by Master Li (Liangjie), he attained great enlightenment.

Some time later, while walking in meditation at night, he heard two monks discussing the karmic cause regarding Old Huanglong’s "Buddha-hand and Donkey-foot. Finding this extraordinary, he went to question them:
"Where does Master Nan now reside? They replied, "He is at Huangbo. At dawn, he went straight to Master Nan; upon meeting him, they conversed.

Feeling that he was still not yet equal to the task, he went to see Cuiyan Zhen Dianxiong. Just as Ying was entering the room, Zhen asked, "How is the meaning of 'a woman emerging from meditative concentration'?
Ying reached out his hand, pinched Zhen’s knee, and departed. Zhen laughed and said, "The customer who sells spoons and chopsticks has not yet arrived.
From this point on, Zhen recognized that Ying’s wit and eloquence were free and unconfined by conventional molds, and he praised him greatly. At... [text ends]

This was the principle followed by scholars of that time. Later, when Nan-pu presided over the assembly at Yuan-tong, whenever he saw a monk coming from Mount Lu, he would invariably ask, "Have you ever paid your respects to Elder Ying?

To those who did not know him, he would say, "If you have traveled on pilgrimage to Mount Lu and do not know Elder Ying, this is what is called returning empty-handed from a precious mountain. Such was Nan-pu while he was in the world.
He was unwilling to open the Dharma [to the public]. When Master Nán passed away, the Teacher said, "The Great Dharma has been entrusted to me;
who else could bear its responsibility? He subsequently entered the world to reside at Letan. He composed many verses and sayings;

here I record only three of them, by which one may discern his character: "The path of Shimen is perilous, the iron gate secure; Lifting my eyes, ten-thousand-fathom heights rise layer upon layer. [No further verse provided.]

The horned iron ox charges through it, breaking it apart; within the ocean of Vairocana, waves and billows surge. It is also said: An iron caltrop from the furnace of ten thousand smeltings—its price must be high;
do not yield to it. Coming crosswise and going upright, he laughs "he-he"; let others at their leisure stir up right and wrong. It is also said:
The ten directions appear simultaneously upon the tip of a single hair; the Flower Treasury is layered upon layer, as cold as a celestial net. Precious.
"Where has the virtuous youth Sudhana gone? On this clear night, the wind shakes the azure *langgan* (bamboo).

Master Daguan once laughed privately at those who practice Chan without inquiring into principle (*li*). For instance, within the Gate of the Patriarchs (*Zongmen*), there are four ways of concealing the blade:

the first is called "concealing according to principle," the second is "concealing according to phenomena" (*shi*), and when both principle and phenomena are concealed, it is called "entering the concealment. Both...

If one does not engage with both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), it is called "coming out and going toward" (*chujiu*). That [master] did not look at the characters before suddenly shifting to principle;

he made "coming out" easy for "going toward" and "going out" easy for "entering toward. To make "entering toward" serve the phenomenon (*shi*) is not something that can be easily changed; thus, he acted according to his own command.

In the past, you failed to realize that the false attachment to the body as a self-characteristic gives rise to emotions such as love and hatred. Following these emotions, one creates karma;

following karma, one receives retribution. Thus, through birth, old age, sickness, and death, one transmigrates through the cycle of samsara for long kalpas. Yet, the enlightened nature within the body has never undergone birth or death.
It is like being driven about in a dream; the body is originally at ease and tranquil, yet it is like water turning to ice, its moist nature remaining unchanged.
If one can awaken to this meaning, that is the Dharmakāya. It is fundamentally unborn from the beginning—how could there be any dependence or support?

It is luminous and never obscured, clearly and eternally cognizant. It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere. Nevertheless, due to the habitual delusions of many lifetimes, one clings to it as if it were an established nature.
Joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure flow in subtle currents. Although the True Principle is sharp and penetrating, these emotions are difficult to eliminate abruptly;
one must maintain constant vigilance and diminish them further and further. It is like the wind suddenly ceasing and the waves gradually subsiding.

How could the practice of a single body be identical to the functioning of a Buddha? One may only take emptiness and stillness as one's own essence, and must not identify with the physical body. By means of the Truth...
Know that [all] is one's own mind; do not identify with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Then, at the time of death, natural karma will be unable to bind you.
Although there may be an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), your destination will be free and unfettered; whether in the heavens or among humans, you may take up residence as you wish.
If love and hatred have already been extinguished, you will not receive a body of segmented existence (*prādeśika-śarīra*). Naturally, you will transform the short for the long.
Long ago, it was easy to transform the coarse into the subtle; now that the subtle flow has ceased, all things are utterly tranquil and extinguished.

Only the great wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment remains, radiantly solitary. It then manifests as hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies according to conditions to deliver sentient beings with whom there is a karmic affinity;

this is what is called a Buddha. In our own dynasty, the Minister Han Zonggu once sent a letter inquiring of the Venerable Master Haitang, saying: "I have previously heard that you, Master, attained enlightenment."
"I am vast and free from doubt. However, since beginningless time, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of affliction have not yet been suddenly exhausted. What should be done about this?
Huitang replied: "I respectfully acknowledge what you have written regarding your past awakening and your state of being vast and free from doubt.
As for the fact that the habitual tendencies of affliction from beginningless time have not yet been suddenly exhausted—yet, as there is no dharma remaining outside the mind..."
To recognize what the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions are and then desire to exhaust them—if one gives rise to such a mind, it is instead like mistaking a thief for one's own son.
From the time of the ancient masters onward, all verbal teachings have been medicines prescribed according to specific ailments.

Even if there were habitual tendencies of affliction, they were treated solely with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; these were all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) used to guide and lead [beings].
[The Master] said: "If there were truly habit-energies (*vāsanā*) that could be treated, it would mean that there are dharmas existing outside the mind that can be exhausted.

This is like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail through the mud; as one wipes away the tracks, new tracks arise. One might say this is 'using the mind to employ the mind,' which only serves to reveal the depth of one's illness.
If you can clearly realize that there are no dharmas outside the mind and no mind outside dharmas, then since both mind and dharmas are non-existent, what further instruction could there be?"
Who could ever exhaustively fathom this? I humbly submit this brief response to your instructions, intended merely as a letter from the mountains.

These two elders are the ancestral masters of both ancient and modern times; their skillful means, applied as appropriate to the occasion, possess an inherent flavor. From the outset, there has been no question of superiority or inferiority between them.
However, the words with which Guifeng responded precisely captured the intent of what Master Han had asked; his expression did not lose its fundamental principle and opened up correct insight.
When compared with the Esoteric (Mijiao), that which Huìtáng attained was far more extensive.
Master Yongming said: "As for the true lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, who can truly recognize it? However, as long as one has a place of faith, one may become a teacher for others.
If we discuss the gate of cultivation and realization, all quarters say that one's merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages;

yet, according to what is permitted within the teachings, even those bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind can be compared and understood through them, and it is also permitted to reach an understanding by relying on the teachings—first, through hearing."
Entering through understanding and faith. Subsequently, one accords with this through non-thinking. If one enters the gate of faith, one immediately ascends to the rank of the Patriarch.
Now, taking present-worldly matters as an illustration within the realm of sentient beings, there are three ways of knowing: first, knowledge by inference; second, direct perception;
and third, knowledge through the teachings. Regarding the first, knowledge by inference: for example, this very body of outflows (āsrava) currently possesses [sleep] every night.
A dream: the favorable and unfavorable objects perceived within a dream, with their attendant sorrows and joys, appear vividly;
yet upon awakening, one sleeps peacefully upon the bed—how could they have ever been real? All are produced by the mental consciousness and its conceptualizations within the dream.

By this analogy, one may know that the things seen during the waking state are all as unreal as those in a dream. Thus, the objects of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—[are likewise unreal].
Originally, these are the direct objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* and are transformed solely by this fundamental consciousness.

If they are objects of the present, they are discriminated by the clear and distinct *manovijñāna*; if they are objects of the past or future, they are conceptualized by the solitary and dispersed *manovijñāna*.
Although the objects of dreams and waking differ, both do not transcend the *manovijñāna*. Thus, the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) is established.

The analogy is clear. Second, regarding what is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): this refers to things that are manifest before one, requiring no further illustration by means of analogy.
For instance, when one presently perceives objects that are blue or white, the objects themselves are fundamentally empty; they do not say, "I am blue" or "I am white.

It is entirely the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) acting in conjunction with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that discriminates and conceptualizes them as blue or white. It is the mind that identifies them as "form" (*rūpa*).

To designate something as "blue" through verbal expression is entirely a product of mental discourse (*manojalpa*), a false construction established by oneself. Because the six sense objects are insentient, their substance does not establish itself;

names do not call themselves forth. Just as it is with a single form, so it is with all phenomena: they are all devoid of intrinsic nature and are entirely products of mental discourse. Therefore it is said:
"The ten thousand dharmas are originally tranquil, yet people themselves create turmoil. Thus, when a thought arises, the ten thousand...

All objects possess [this nature]. If the mind is empty, the locus where it arises is such that the myriad objects are all empty; thus, emptiness is not empty of itself, but is empty because of the mind.
Existence is not existent of itself, but is existent because of the mind. Since it is neither empty nor existent, it is merely consciousness and merely mind.
If there were no mind, upon what would the myriad dharmas rely? Furthermore, as for past objects, how could they have ever been existent? They arise only in accordance with recollection.
When the sense objects suddenly appear before one, if thoughts do not arise, the objects will ultimately not manifest.

This is something all sentient beings can know through their daily experience; it does not depend on the perfection of effort, nor is it something to be attained through cultivation. Any being with a mind can verify this for themselves.

Therefore, the former masters said: "One who is like a person of great capacity and knows *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) constantly contemplates their own mind, taking mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) as the object.

Although at this initial stage of contemplation one has not yet attained the factors of a noble being (*ārya-bhūmi*), knowing that mental verbalization is the object constitutes what is called 'knowing through the third [stage] according to the teachings' for a bodhisattva.
As the *Mahāyāna-sūtra* states: "The triple world is mind-only; all phenomena are consciousness-only. This is the fundamental principle to be realized.

This is the primary meaning of the definitive teaching. I have repeatedly contemplated these words three times over, sighing that what the Buddhas and Patriarchs have revealed is so vast and level, clear and simple;
yet, few truly believe it. Why is this? As National Teacher Qingliang said:
"Practitioners should diligently apply themselves to mindfulness and knowledge regarding the rituals of manifest cultivation, for they are attached to worldly affairs. There is no...
It is exceedingly difficult to abandon long-standing evil habits; they are harder to part from than a worldly compassionate father is for his filial son.
Therefore, one must apply diligent effort (*vīrya*) to be able to eliminate them. Through diligence, one desires to exert oneself with earnest encouragement, being brave and tireless.

Through mindfulness (*smṛti*), one clearly remembers without forgetting. Through knowledge (*jñāna*), one makes decisive judgments without regret. I vow to uphold the instructions of Qingliang and follow the intent of Yongming.
Accompanied by his fellow practitioners, he entered the Hall of Perfect Quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).
Initially, Song Mingjiao had traveled from Dongshan to Mount Kang, where he took up residence at the Dharma seat of Kaixian.
The presiding master, noting that he was an excellent youth and keenly devoted to literature, appointed him as Secretary. Mingjiao smiled and said, "How could I do this for you?"

"Is this ginger-and-apricot soup? he asked, and because of this, [Zhao] set it aside. He resided at West Lake in Hangzhou for thirty years, keeping his doors closed and not engaging in idle social intercourse.

During the Jiayou era, he presented to the imperial court the *Fujiao bian* (Compilation on Aiding the Teachings), the *Dingzu tu* (Chart of the Fixed Lineage), and the *Zengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage), which he had composed.

At that time, the Honorable Wang Su of the Hanlin Academy was acting as the Governor of Kaifeng. He submitted a memorial on Mingjiao’s behalf to the court, and Emperor Renzong marveled at it for a long time.
The document was forwarded to the Secretariat, where Prime Minister Han Gong and State Councilor Ouyang Gong read his writings and were greatly astonished.
They praised him among the court officials and gentlemen, and the work was eventually granted entry into the imperial canon. Thus, Mingjiao’s fame spread throughout the world.
In the evening, he moved his residence to the Yong’an Hermitage north of Lingyin. At dawn, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing his voice.
After his midday meal, he read scriptures; when guests arrived, he engaged in pure conversation, never discussing worldly affairs.
He once said: "When guests depart, pure conversation diminishes; as years advance, white hair abounds. At midnight, he would recite the name of Avalokiteśvara ten thousand times.
He would then retire to bed. His austere and frugal lifestyle was sufficient to rival that of Sengyuan of Mount Zhong.
I once saw a letter he had written by hand to Master Yue, which said: "For several years I have wished to make a paper quilt to ward off the bitter cold;
now, fortunately, it is finished. I imagine you will laugh heartily upon hearing of this. When his end approached, he sat upright with a smile and requested [to be moved].
He composed a verse, saying: "The moon is bright at the beginning of the latter night; I shall go forth alone.

I do not emulate the old man of Damei, Who still craves the cries of the flying squirrel. The Master received the Dharma from Chan Master Dongshan Cong, yet the lineage charts place him among the dharma heirs of Deshan Yuan. This is an error.

On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Huangyou era, Emperor Renzong issued an imperial decree to Chan Master Dajue.

He proceeded to the Rear Garden and partook of a vegetarian feast at Huacheng Hall. Upon the conclusion of the feast, an imperial edict was proclaimed that he should follow the ritual protocols of the Chan monasteries of the South to open the hall and expound the Dharma.
Furthermore, an edict was issued for Qingman, the Great Master Ciyun and Vice Registrar of the Left Street, to deliver the formal invocation. After Man had expressed his gratitude, he proclaimed:
"The spring has returned to the Imperial Garden, and the assembly of the Royal House has been convened. Since the Ten-Thousand-Wagon Sovereign has arrived at the Palace of Shun, the two [monks]..."
Jiehui has received this honor from Yao Mei. Now that we are at this season of harmony and warmth, it is precisely the day for proclaiming and exalting [the Dharma].

It is fitting to discuss the Way of our Ancestors so as to fully satisfy the Imperial heart. This is respectfully submitted. Lian then ascended the seat. After the exchange of questions and answers was concluded, he said:

"Within the hall of the Ancient Buddhas, there has never been any divergent teaching; yet within the phrases used for circulation, there are indeed many discourses. Those who attain them will find their wondrous function remains unimpaired."

Those who lose this find themselves stalled at every turn. Thus, by streams and mountains, clouds and moon, the same breeze blows everywhere; by water-birds and forest trees, the Way is revealed at every step.
If one enters the gate of Mahākāśyapa, it is as if the wind of Yao sweeps vast and clear, and the sun of Shun shines with brilliant clarity.
The village elders sing their praises and the fishermen dance with joy. At such a time, there is nothing but the transformation of pure, non-action. How could it be otherwise?
Knowing that such a matter existed, the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased.
Du Qigong and Zhang Wen Ding had both retired from office and were residing in Suizhou. They frequented one another’s quarters in the village lanes.
There was a man named Zhu Chengshi who traveled between the two elders for the purpose of providing medical care. Qigong was upright and strict, never mixing with heterodox studies; whenever...
Xiao An mocked the Master’s devotion to Buddhism whenever he encountered guests, invariably using this to ridicule him. Wen Ding merely smiled.
Attendant Zhu took the opportunity to say to Wen Ding, "Master Du is a great man of the world; it is a pity that he does not yet know of this matter.
You have the power to do so—why not encourage him to awaken to it? Wen Ding replied, "Your karmic affinity with this old man is stronger than mine. I shall stop here."
"I can only assist you. Zhu Zhe replied and departed. One day, Lord Qi summoned Zhu and examined his pulse with great urgency.
Zhu said to the messenger, "Go first and inform the Prime Minister, saying only that I have not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The messenger reported this as instructed. Lord Qi remained silent for a long while before arriving. He leaned on his armrest, bowed to Zhu, and invited him to sit. Then, he spoke slowly:
"I, an old man, have always regarded you as a man of broad learning and refined understanding. I did not expect that recently you too would fall into the ranks of the mediocre and vulgar.
As for what is called the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, what kind of discourse is it that you are so obsessed with? The subtle words of the sages do not exceed those of Confucius and Mencius.

To abandon these and take up that other is a great delusion. Zhu replied, "Since Your Excellency has not yet read this scripture, how can you know that it does not equal the teachings of Confucius and Mencius?"
"From my perspective," he said, "it seems this is an error. He drew the first scroll from his sleeve and said, "Minister, please examine it.
Lord Qi scrutinized the text; having no choice, he took it and read it silently, unaware that he had finished the entire roll.

Suddenly, he rose in great alarm and exclaimed, "How could such a book exist in this world? He dispatched a messenger to bring all the remaining scrolls, and having read them through, he seized [the author].
Zhushou said, "You are truly my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Why did you not tell me earlier, even though An Dao had known of this for a long time?
He immediately ordered his carriage to visit Wen Ding and recounted the matter. An Dao said, "It is like a person who has lost an object and suddenly finds it;
one should simply rejoice in having found it. One must not regret whether it was found early or late. I, [the speaker],...
"It was not that I failed to inform you; rather, because your karmic affinity with Master Zhu was deep, I sent him instead.
Even when Buddhas and patriarchs transform beings, they must rely on those with whom they share common karma. Lord Qi was greatly pleased.
Chan Master Shanshi of Fuchang in Jingzhou was the spiritual son of Master Mingjiao Kuan. He was a man of reverent dignity who held the Great Dharma in profound secrecy.
When he first took up residence there, the monastery consisted of only ten or so dilapidated buildings and merely three or four remaining monks.

Yet Shanshi offered incense at dawn and lit lamps at dusk, ascending the hall to preach the Dharma as if presiding over a thousand-fold assembly; furthermore, all the necessary provisions and implements appropriate for a monastic community were fully provided.
He prepared his quarters for visitors; when travelers arrived, he received them with solemn reverence. It was only after more than ten years that disciples began to gather.
The whole world turned toward him with longing admiration. Master Nan and Master Yue were also among the assembly. One day, Master Nan said, "I have been ill with a cold and am taking medicine;
I must cover myself with a quilt to induce perspiration. He sent Wen Yue to borrow one throughout the monastery, but among the more than a hundred people there, none had one.
In the past, one used paper for this; nowadays it is not so. Upon thick felt, one covers it with a cushion.
To wake up three times a day—this may truly be called a joyful age.
The *Huayan lun* states: "If one follows the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the myriad marks are entirely non-existent; if one follows the power of wisdom, the various marks appear accordingly.

Manifestation and concealment follow conditions, yet there is no creator at all. Ordinary beings cling to this and thereby produce ignorance (*avidyā*). Since these attachments and obstructions are fundamentally non-existent..."
The function of wisdom is sovereign. Chan Master Yongming said: "Without departing from the realm of the single truth, the modes of transformation manifest in a hundred variations.
Thus, when an arrow pierces a stone tiger, it is not due to human effort; when one in intoxication issues commands to the three armies, how could that be produced by yeast or malt?
When bamboo shoots emerge from a cold valley, they are not born of the warm springtime; when fish leap from icy rivers, how could they be caught by nets?"
Thus, all things are moved by the mind; this spiritual penetration is thereby manifested. Therefore, one knows that the functioning of the myriad dharmas is entirely the power of one's own mind.
Chan Master Xuánmíng of Jīnfēng was a successor of Chan Master Tánzhāng of Cáo shān. His countenance was extraordinary and ancient, and his intellectual eloquence was profound.
One day, Guanzhong ascended the seat and said: "The matter lies in the meeting of lid and box; the principle should be like the point of an arrow striking its target.
If anyone can speak thus, I shall grant them half the monastery. At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly. Ming stepped down from his seat, detained him, and said:
"It is easy to meet as friends, but it is difficult to serve together as men of the Way. Begone!"

When Chan Master Daben reached the age of eighty, he passed away at Lingyan Mountain in Suzhou. As he was about to depart, his disciples requested, saying, "The Master’s teachings have spread throughout the world;
today you must leave behind a verse as an instruction. Daben sat upright and gazed intently at them, saying, "You foolish children!
Even in my ordinary days I am too lazy to compose verses; what are you trying to achieve by making such a special effort today? When I usually wish to lie down," he said, [he simply does so].
He lay down, saying, "I cannot sit upright today for this specific purpose. He then took paper and brush and wrote five characters in large script: "My final affairs are entrusted to Shou-rong.
Having cast aside his brush, he lay down in a daze as if in deep sleep. When they shook him, he was already gone.

Regarding the two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: first, the transformation of defilement into purity; second, the transformation of delusion into awakening.

Bodhi is "attained through birth" (*utpatti-labdha*), meaning that because the two obstacles previously prevented its arising, now that the obstacles have been severed, it is termed "attained through birth.

Nirvāṇa is termed "attained through manifestation" (*abhisamaya-labdha*); its original nature is pure, yet it was obscured by adventitious dust. Now that [the dust] has been severed and it is revealed, it is called "manifestation."
Yes, it is attained. However, there are six stages of transformation. First is the transformation that diminishes power and augments capacity.

This refers to the first two stages, wherein by means of the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), one diminishes the force of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and augments the functional capacity of the pure seeds, thereby gradually subduing their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

It is also called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*). Second is the transformation of thorough penetration: by the power of penetrating the truth through the path of seeing, one abandons the coarse aspects of the two obstacles and realizes a portion of the true transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Third is the transformation of cultivation: this refers to the gradual abandonment of innate [afflictions] stage by stage.
This is the transformation based on realizing the truth (*tattva*). Fourth is the transformation of the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala-paripūri-parāvṛtti*):

this refers to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), wherein by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), one eternally severs all innate heavy obscurations (*dausthulya*) and suddenly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood; it is the transformation of the fulfillment [of the fruit]. Fifth is the inferior transformation (*hīna-parāvṛtti*).

This refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who, weary of suffering and longing for tranquility, realize the true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); because they lack superior capability, [this is not the case]. Sixth is the "Vast Transformation":

this refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna, where there is neither longing nor weariness, one penetrates the two kinds of emptiness, simultaneously abandons the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), and suddenly realizes unsurpassed bodhi;
because it possesses superior capability, [it is so called].
A monk of the Tang dynasty, styled Làn Zàn, lived in seclusion within a stone cave atop Mount Heng.

He once composed a song, the gist of which was: "The affairs of the world are wearying; they are not as good as the mountain peaks. Reclining beneath the wisteria vines, with a block of stone for a pillow.

His words were grand and profound, all revealing the mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. When Emperor Dēngzō heard of his reputation, he dispatched a messenger on horseback to issue an imperial decree summoning him. The messenger...

He went directly to the cave and proclaimed: "The Son of Heaven has issued an imperial decree; Venerable Sir, please arise to express your gratitude. Sengzan was just then stirring up a fire of cow dung to roast yams to eat;
with cold tears streaming down his chest, he did not respond at all. The messenger laughed at him and urged him to wipe away his tears.
Sengzan said, "How could I have the leisure to wipe away the tears of a worldly person? In the end, he could not be brought [to the court].

He departed. Emperor Dezong admired and sighed in praise of him. I have once beheld his portrait; with a drooping chin and glaring eyes, its spirit and resonance transcend the mundane, appearing as one who cannot be easily provoked or approached.
I inscribed upon it: "The dung-fire knows only the excellence of the yellow tuber;
How could those silver hooks recognize the fresh purple clay seal? I still lack the mental composure to wipe away cold tears; How could I have the leisure to inquire after worldly folk?"
The Vinaya section states: Long ago, there was a kingdom in great turmoil, and the people vied with one another to flee to other lands. The houses along the roadside were all empty.
An old soldier passed by and heard the sound of wailing; he entered to look and saw an infant gazing up at the rafters of the roof.
The veteran soldier followed and observed it; it was merely a cord with rice suspended from it. He untied it and showed it to him—it was ash. Upon seeing this, the infant died immediately.
It appears that his mother, wishing to abandon him but unable to bear killing him, had hung this cord and deceived him by saying, "This is rice.
Thus, his mental focus remained fixed on it without forgetting, and once he recognized it as ash, no further thoughts arose. From this, one comes to know the three realms.

The stagnation within birth and death is entirely sustained by conceptualization. Thus, when the great adepts of old who had mastered the Dharma attained a state of transcendent self-mastery at the moment of death, it was not due to any other path;
they simply realized the fundamental source of consciousness.
The monastic communities have handed down the tradition that when Master Shitou offered his body as food to tigers, he made this vow:
"If my school should flourish greatly in the future, it shall first consume my feet. Indeed, the tigers began eating from his feet. I privately laughed at this.

At the beginning of the Shaosheng era, while traveling to Nantai, I saw the monk T'ai performing a ritual for Shitou; in his text commemorating the event, the Venerable Ming described the offering of his body to the tigers in great detail.
Upon careful examination, one realizes that later generations were unable to clarify this, and consequently transmitted the tradition that it was Master Xuanzang.
It is also said that when Chan Master Qingliang Fayen was nearing death, he wrote a letter to part from Lord Li. When the Lord visited his residence, Fayen would not leave;
his attendant then pressed him down with a sack of rice, and only then did he pass away. According to his original biography, Fayen died in the fifth year of the Xuande era of the Zhou dynasty.

On the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the year Wumu, he manifested illness. In the intercalary month, he shaved his head and bathed; then, having addressed the assembly, he passed away while seated. He had never previously sent a letter to inform the State Preceptor (Guozhu) of his intention. Yet, when Han Xizai composed the Stele Inscription for Chan Master Wukong, he stated: [The inscription says: "In the seventh month of the year Wumu, on the seventeenth day, the Master manifested illness. In the intercalary month, he shaved his head and bathed. He then informed the assembly and sat until his passing. He had never before sent a letter to inform the State Preceptor. However, this was not the case. Furthermore, the inscription continues: "At that time, the State Preceptor was residing at the Great Xiangguo Temple. Upon hearing of the Master’s passing, he immediately dispatched the monk Daoying to offer condolences and present gifts. The Master received them with a smile and said, 'I am merely returning to my original source. There is no need for such formalities. This account, however, contradicts the historical record. It is likely that Han Xizai, being a close friend of the Master, embellished these details out of affection. Moreover, the Master had already been ill for some time prior to the intercalary month; it is simply that the specific date of his death was recorded in the official chronicles. Thus, we know that the Master did not send a letter to the State Preceptor beforehand. As for the claim that the Master “sat until his passing” (zuoshi), this is a common expression used by the Buddhist community to describe the manner of a master’s final departure. It does not mean that he remained seated for the duration of his life. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the inscription and the historical records. Furthermore, the inscription states: "The Master was originally from the region of Hengzhou. His secular surname was Chen, and his given name was Zhen. His father, Chen Shou, served as the Magistrate of Zhaoling County. When the Master was young, he was already exceptionally intelligent and possessed a profound disposition. At the age of twelve, he left home to become a novice under Master Daohui of the Daxiangguo Temple in the capital. Later, he traveled to the mountain hermitages of the various masters of the Chan school, seeking instruction and refining his practice. By the time he reached the age of twenty-four, he had attained great realization. Subsequently, he returned to the capital and resided at the Daxiangguo Temple. The State Preceptor, deeply impressed by his virtue, appointed him as the Abbot of the temple. The Master declined the honor, saying, 'I am but a man of humble talent and shallow learning. How could I presume to occupy this position? The State Preceptor insisted, saying, 'The Master's reputation has spread far and wide. Your refusal would only cause me further distress. The Master finally accepted. From then on, he led the assembly with great dignity, and his influence extended throughout the realm. Monks and laypeople alike flocked to him from all directions. Whenever he preached the Dharma, the listeners were moved to tears. His disciples numbered over a thousand. In the year Wuyin, the State Preceptor was transferred to the Great Xiangguo Temple. The Master followed him there and continued to serve as the Abbot. In the year Wuzi, the State Preceptor retired to the Tongtai Temple. The Master again followed him there and resided as the Abbot. In the year Wushen, the State Preceptor passed away. The Master remained at the Tongtai Temple, continuing to teach and transform others. In the year Wuyu, he manifested illness and passed away at the Daxiangguo Temple. This account is largely consistent with the historical records. However, the inscription further states: "The Master was fond of composing poetry and was skilled in calligraphy. His writings were collected into two volumes, titled the *Wukong Chanshi Ji*. His calligraphy was admired by both the clergy and the laity. He was also well-versed in the Vinaya and the Mahayana sutras. He often lectured on the *Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra* and the *Vimalakirti Sutra*, and his explanations were clear and penetrating. He also composed the *Shishi Yaoji* (Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma) in ten fascicles, which circulated widely among the world. This is also in accord with the historical records. Furthermore, the inscription states: "In the year Wuyu, the State Preceptor was transferred to the Great Xiangguo Temple. The Master followed him there and resided as the Abbot. In the year Wuzi, the State Preceptor retired to the Tongtai Temple. The Master again followed him there and resided as the Abbot. In the year Wushen, the State Preceptor passed away. Today, it is being sold by merchants throughout the world, yet scholars often spend their entire lives [without seeing it].
Those who have never recognized this find the Dharma trivial, and thus their seeds of faith are naturally inferior—how lamentable!
Ancient monks dwelling in the mountains often used objects to convey their meaning; they did so both for their own playful expression and to awaken others.
For example, there was Zi Hu’s keeping of a dog, and Dao Wu’s wearing a sorcerer’s robe and holding official tablets; yet Xuefeng, Guizong, and Xiuan Yuan all likewise held [the staff].
A wooden snake. Thus, Xuefeng sent a verse to Xiuyuan, saying: "A man who dwells in his true colors leaves no trace of axe or hatchet.
During the Yuanyufu era, I went to Shushan and saw that the portrait of Master Ren also held a wooden snake.
Once, a monk asked him, "What is this object in your hand, Master? He replied, "It is Cao’s daughter," and sighed over its solitude.
Its resonance is transcendent and sublime; it can cool the heat of affliction. He composed a hymn in its praise, saying: "The habitual tendencies of the three branches burn with fierce poison;
they permeate and steam the consciousness-mind, coiling and entangling it. Sentient beings, lacking clarity, give rise to groundless doubts and fears;

upon suddenly beholding this, they are instantly struck down by terror. Yet the world of empty flowers is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing; vast and open, the ten directions reveal their hidden caverns."
I consider my junior uncle, Master Ai, to be a great master of illusion. He freely bestows and takes away the myriad dharmas for his own playful amusement;
thus one knows that the great trichiliocosm is but a toy for his play. The wooden snake in his hand is none other than the daughter of Cao.
Master Yongming asked: "This fundamental consciousness-mind is called the essence-body of all phenomena, and it is also said to be eternally abiding and immovable.
Now, as for the myriad phenomena: do they exist within this single mind, or do they exist apart from this single mind?

If they are identical to the mind, then since the myriad phenomena are subject to change and transformation, how can this mind be called eternally abiding? If they are separate from this mind, then again, how [can they be its essence]?"
It is established as the essence of all phenomena. He answers himself: "Opening and closing follow conditions; they are neither identical nor separate. Because conditions assemble, there is closing;

because conditions disperse, there is opening. Opening and closing are merely conditions; their contraction and expansion have no intrinsic substance. Conditions merely open and close, yet conditions themselves are fundamentally empty.
Subject and object are mutually unknowing; both the agent and the object are quiescent. Thus, a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says: "For example, like gold..."
Rocks and the like originally possess no quality of water; yet when they are combined with water, if the water flows, the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise.
Its essence is not flowing, yet it flows as it is associated with the various consciousnesses and turns along with phenomena.
Just as iron moves around due to a magnet, both are devoid of volition, yet they appear as if they possessed thought and awareness. Thus it is with the *ālaya*.
The seven consciousnesses should be known to be likewise: bound by the ropes of habitual tendencies, they appear to exist though there is no person;
they pervade the bodies of all sentient beings and circulate through the various aggregates and realms of existence.

Just as iron and the magnet do not know one another, yet interact, I have observed that all sentient beings are deluded amidst movement, transition, and shifting, giving rise to a mind of attachment that takes these to be real.
However, because of these false calculations of birth and death, and of sinful or meritorious actions, it is like an infant spinning around and seeing the house rotate.

Out of great compassion, the Buddhas employ skillful means: by using the fact that insentient things lack mental consciousness yet still undergo flux as an analogy, they demonstrate that the fundamental nature of the conscious mind is originally quiescent.
Thus, one immediately enters the Great Gate of Liberation of Non-arising.
On Mount Dawu in Tanzhou there was a deep pool where a venomous dragon lay dormant. If a fallen leaf disturbed its waves, thunder and rain would follow for days on end;
those who passed by dared not even draw breath. Ciming and Quandao were traveling together when Quandao tugged at Ciming’s robe, saying, "We should bathe together.
Ciming pulled back his arm and walked straight away. Quandao took off his clothes and leaped in; a clap of thunder followed immediately, and a stench-carrying wind blew down the rain.
The forest trees were tossed about. Ciming crouched amidst the grass, greatly alarmed, thinking that Yiquan must have died. After a short while, the sky cleared and brightened;
suddenly, [Yiquan] extended his neck out from between the waves and called out with a laugh, "Qi! Once, while sitting at night on the summit of Mount Rong, a large python coiled around him.
Yiquan untied his sash and bound it around the snake's waist. By midnight, it was nowhere to be seen. At dawn, he took up his staff and searched throughout the mountain.
It was bound with a girdle upon a withered pine tree; it was, in fact, a pine-spirit. Furthermore, he carried a stone statue of an Arhat from the Rear Cave to the Southern Terrace.
The statue weighed several hundred *jin*, yet the monks were struck with awe and did not know how it had arrived. The monks of the Rear Cave likewise did not know how it had departed.
Thus, the tradition has been passed down to this day, and it is known as the "Flying-Arived Arhat. He then proceeded to Mount Heng.
In a certain county, he saw a butcher hacking meat. He stood by his side, assuming an expression of piteous distress, pointing first to the meat and then to his own mouth.
The butcher asked, "Are you mute? whereupon he nodded his head. The butcher took great pity on him, cut off a large piece of meat, and placed it in his bowl.
Quanxi was delighted that this exceeded his expectations. He called out repeatedly, "Thank you! The townspeople all laughed, but Quanxi went on his way as if nothing had happened.
Later, while staying at the Bajiao Hermitage on Mount Nanyue, he encountered misfortune. His clothes were stripped from him and he was conscripted into the labor service of the Chenzhou fortress.

During the height of summer, while carrying earth to build the city walls, he reached the main thoroughfare; he set down his burden and sat there. Onlookers gathered like a wall around him. He spoke a verse, saying: "This morning..."
On the sixth day of the sixth month, Guquan’s retribution was fulfilled; he would either ascend to heaven or enter hell.

Having said this, he smiled and passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the air. The people of Ch’en continue to make offerings to him to this day. Guquan had personally seen the Chan Master Wude of Fenzhou.
Later, the practitioner Qingyuan of Nanshan said to me: "For over ten years, I acted as an old monk..."
The attendant Long had heard his account of the events concerning Ciming in great detail. He once sighed with emotion, saying:

The teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are wholesome medicine; a defiled mind is a mixture of poison.
If one cannot avoid it, the disease of birth and death will never be diminished. I cherish these words and recall the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says:
"If sentient beings in the final age do not give rise to false thoughts in their minds, the Buddha says that such people are Bodhisattvas in this very life. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

Fist. It is not that there is no fist; yet it does not know knowing, nor does it know itself as knowing.

Just as when a hand does not grasp an object and does not itself form a fist, it cannot be said to be without hands, for the hand remains intact; thus it is not the same as a rabbit’s horn. —Master Zhijue.

It is said: This constitutes the subtlety of the Chan school; therefore, although it is employed here now, there are slight differences. For that [Chan] school merely reveals non-conditioned true wisdom as the true path.

"Regarding matters of clan, lineage, hometown, and local customs—would you truly take them to heart? When I read to this point, I know that what Mingjiao has attained is much indeed.

how much less so the fame left after death? This is like Master Liang’s escape to the Western Mountains, or Master Chang’s hermitage."
Dàmé, Guīzōng’s blinding of his eyes, and Fǎzhèng’s refusal to state his name or surname—these elders were all able to put into practice what they had heard.
Therefore, even several hundred years after their passing, they still possess a formidable, living vitality.
They were indifferent to the struggles of this world; it was for this reason that they were granted such stature. This is simply the natural order of things.

as soon as there is the slightest entry of deliberation, it ceases to be efficacious. My old friend Zou Zhengchen of Yexi was able to discourse on the Five Elements."
Those who are refined and subtle in this world may be counted by the tens or twenties; they have also once told me of this principle.
If even those who have reached the pinnacle of such arts are like this, how much more so for that which is greater than this—how could one seek it through discursive thought?
The abbot Deng Fengyong once asked the monk Shenqi, "It has been a long time since we last met; what have you been doing?
Qi replied, "Recently I saw Abbot Wei and discovered a place of peace and happiness. Yong said, "Try explaining it to me. Qi then recounted what he had attained.
Yong said, "You are right, but Wei is not. Qi did not understand this and returned to tell Wei. Wei laughed heartily and said, "You..."
"No, it is not. It has never been 'not. Qi went to consult Master Jicui Nan; Master Nan also laughed heartily.
When Yong heard of this, he composed a verse: "Light and darkness intermingle—the mechanism of killing and giving life. This is the realm of the Great Man, known by Samantabhadra.
Born from the same root, yet dying on different branches—laughing until one collapses, that ancient adept within the hermitage. Observing his words, one can imagine [the spirit of] that time.
If Master Yong were to apply the elegant resonance of the Dharma-joy that delights in play to the present day, he would surely incur reproach and humiliation.
The verse with which the Great Master Linji transmitted the Dharma at the time of his death says: "Following the current without ceasing, one asks: 'How is it? True illumination has no..."

He spoke to him as if explaining it to another: "Free from characteristics and free from names, it is like not having received instruction. 'When the razor has been used, one must quickly sharpen it'—the transmitter took this to mean 'one must quickly return to sharpening.
