When the message is exhausted, how can one distinguish the clarity within the turbidity? Yet those who transmit it render "exhaustion" as "not exhausted.
These two verses of the two schools are extremely subtle; if even one loses its essential meaning, the harm is very great. Therefore, one must not fail to discern what is being said.
Regarding those who use a *gyūsu* (whistling kettle) for grinding [tea], the boatman said: "One must truly vanish where there is no trace; where there is no trace, do not hide.
When joy and discernment are exhausted, the news is also exhausted. How can a person distinguish the clear within the turbid?
This is what Daguān meant by "the biased and the correct, the horizontal and the vertical. It is far removed from the avoidance of perfection; one must penetrate the Dragon Gate.
The path of birds cannot be traversed; the barren woman weaves in the frost. The clay ox plows within the fire.
If one can be liberated from both ends, it is like a single branch flourishing on a withered tree.
The Layman Wujin once asked me: "Master Wuben composed the 'Verses on the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject.
Regarding the line in the 'Coming from within the Center' that says, 'One need only not touch upon the current taboo;

it is even better than knowing the talent of the one who had his tongue cut off by the court,' although the intention of the former masters is clear and subtle, there must be a basis for the claim that the one from the Zhao dynasty had his tongue cut off. Yet, it is said that among those of antiquity, there was no such instance."
Regarding the matter of the tongue: moreover, to say "he knew the court" is even more meaningless. Is this not perhaps an error in the transmission of later records? I said:
The old edition reads, "He surpassed the talent of those who were cut-tongued in previous courts.

This likely refers to Shu, the father of He Ruo Bi of the Sui dynasty, who was killed by Yuwen Hu because he was suspected of being harmful. As he faced execution, he warned him, saying: "I have died because of my tongue; [I would] lead you..."
He pierced Bi’s tongue with an awl until it bled, intending to make him guard his speech. Before the rise of the Tang and during the Sui dynasty, the former court practiced piercing the tongue;
this was not a sign of an enlightened administration. Nevertheless, the intent behind cutting the tongue and piercing the tongue is the same. Wujin requested that I record this for him.

Chan Master Daoyuan was a native of Nanxiong Prefecture; his secular surname was Chunzhi. Having traveled extensively as a youth, although he had studied deeply under many masters, he had not yet attained full realization.
Hearing that Chan Master Nan resided at Jicui Hermitage on Huangbo Mountain, he went there to rely upon him.

One day, while sitting in the hall after the formal session had concluded, he heard two monks discussing the karmic account of Baizhang’s “wild fox. One monk said, "As for the phrase, 'Not being oblivious to cause and effect'—"
"You have still not escaped the body of a wild fox. A monk responded at once, saying, "This very state is precisely not falling into cause and effect;
how could one ever have fallen into the body of a wild fox? Yuan was struck with awe by these words and did not even realize that his body had begun to rise.

While walking at the head of Shang’an, he crossed a stream and suddenly attained great enlightenment. When he went to see Master Nan and had not yet finished recounting his experience, tears flowed down to his chin.
Master Nan ordered him to go to the attendant’s bed and sleep soundly. He suddenly rose and composed a verse, saying:
"Not falling, not obscured; Monks and laypeople have no taboos. The man’s spirit is like a king; Who would begrudge the bag, the coverlet, or the single staff?"
"Free and unrestrained! A wild fox leaps into the ranks of the golden-haired lions. Nan-pu laughed heartily for a long time. Later, he composed a verse on the wind and the banner, saying:
"It is neither wind, nor is it a banner; White clouds still cover the green mountains. In my old age, I have truly lost all strength;
I have stolen a moment’s leisure from the midst of busyness. In the past, I heard Yun-an greatly praise this, saying:
His spiritual acumen was no less than that of Master Ying of Shaowu. After Yun’an passed away, I happened to examine his old writings and found these two verses he had personally drafted;
they seemed intended for transmission but remained unfulfilled. I have therefore recorded them here. I have also heard that Master Yuan is currently residing at Xuefeng Temple in Dayu.
The monk Haoyue asked Chan Master Changsha Cen: "Yongjia said, 'When one realizes it, karmic obstacles are originally empty;
when one has not realized it, one must repay past debts. Yet why did the Venerable Siṃha and the Great Master the Second Patriarch also have to repay past debts?
Changsha said, "Virtuous One, you do not understand that they are originally empty. He asked, "What is this original emptiness?"
Lai Kong asked, "Is this the karmic obstruction? Changsha said, "It is. He asked again, "What is the karmic obstruction? Changsha said, "It is primordial emptiness. Thereupon he spoke a verse:
"Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet not non-existent.

The meaning of nirvāṇa as the settling of debts— In its single nature, there is no further distinction. The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* by Nāgārjuna says: "Karma does not arise from conditions... [it does not arise] from...

It is not dependently originated; therefore, it does not exist. Since there is no agent who can initiate karma, and since there is neither karma nor an agent, how could there be the production of a fruit from karma?
If there is no fruit, how could there be one who experiences that karma? Question:

Although you have refuted in various ways karma, its retribution, and the agent who initiates it, we nevertheless see with our own eyes sentient beings performing actions and receiving their retributions. How is this so?

The answer is: Just as when the World-Honored One, through his supernormal powers, creates a manifested person, and that manifested person further creates another manifested person—just like the first manifested person—the former is called the "agent," and that which is created by the manifested person is called "action.
All afflictions and actions are like illusions and dreams, and also like mirages and echoes; thus it was said by Nāgārjuna.

This conveys the meaning of Changsha’s words, which reach the subtle principle of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Wandering through this world, one is as clearly lucid as if in a dream, and as soberly alert as if from within a drunken stupor.
Chan Master Wude of Fenzhou frequently spoke to his disciples about Dongshan’s Five Ranks and Linji’s Three Mysteries.

There is the fundamental matter; all those [teachings] were merely the words used by ancients to establish their gateways. What is there to investigate?
It is just like someone who cannot read characters, holding up a scroll and asking a simpleton about a house. The simpleton says, "This is just paper filled with ink;
why ask me? No child three feet tall would fail to laugh at him. Formerly, there was a monk who asked Xue...
Regarding Master Xuefeng: "Linji had four shouts; what was their intended meaning? Xuefeng replied, "When I first set out on foot, I traveled toward the north of the River.

"I do not yet know this. You should go and ask his descendants. The monk then questioned Nan-yuan regarding the circumstances of Xuefeng having previously dispatched him.
Nan-yuan prostrated himself toward Xuefeng and said, "The Master was truly a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Alas!
Those who nowadays clamor about their own views to others like ignorant children in a house—upon hearing of Xuefeng’s way of employing people, would they not feel a flush of shame upon their faces?
"Is he sweating and coming down with a fever?

When Chan Master Fayun Xiu heard someone approaching with a cloth wrapped around his waist, his facial expression shifted; that man’s intention was already set.
Within the monastic community, how could this be considered shallow? Now, when young bhikṣus see his portrait, they point to it and say, "This was a man who lacked penetration; he is dead."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In all worlds, birth and death continue in succession; birth arises from habitual tendencies, and death results from flux and transformation.
At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and tactile sensation have departed, the good and evil of one's entire life manifest simultaneously.

Ancient commentators have largely omitted this passage, which I consider a source of regret. Upon reading the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, however, I found a meaningful explanation of it, which I now append here.
Below it says: "Regarding the karmic actions of good and evil, when one performs them oneself, why does one not perceive them during that single lifetime?
It is only at the time of casting off one's life that they suddenly manifest. Human life is like a dream; while one is dreaming, how could one know for oneself whether it is a dream or not?
It must wait until the time of awakening for the events within the dream to appear clearly of themselves, without the need for further investigation.

His countenance was stern and cold; solitary, rigid, and outstanding, he was often referred to by the monastic community as "Iron Face.

"I dare not forget your virtue. However, as for the succession of the Dharma, I already have my own teacher. Foyin was inwardly convinced by this;

he had already spoken of it, and since his resolve was firm, he did not change his mind. He subsequently opened the Dharma and became a disciple of Huanglong. His reputation for the Way was preeminent in his time.
He lived constantly with his bag suspended and his staff leaning against the abbot’s quarters, making no plans for the night ahead. The regional commander...

This was most unsuitable for the interior. All the guests marveled at his lofty refinement. He also composed a poem on the mountain:

In winter, he did not use a brazier, but instead made balls from reed flowers (*tǐhuā*) and tucked his feet inside them. When guests arrived, he shared this with them, engaging in endless pure discourse of refined spirit.

Master Linyuan said to me: "There was a layman named Wu Dunfu, who was talented and quick-witted, and who applied himself with keen resolve to the study of the Way.

do you still doubt this? He replied, "I have no doubts. Haichang smiled and said, "Since there is no doubt here, then when that [the body] undergoes transformation and falls, the robes will likewise follow the body naturally;

At that time, his responsive eloquence was like thunder and lightning; it awakened and alerted many who were mired in ignorance and slumber.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith? The Buddha said: 'Subhūti, they are not [ordinary] sentient beings...'"
"Sentient beings, yet not non-sentient beings. Why is this? Subhūti, as for 'sentient beings, sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings;

they are merely named 'sentient beings. This meaning is profound and vast; from the secret intent and subtle essence of the words of the sages of antiquity, scholars have often been bewildered, and the Buddha’s intention remained ultimately unclear.
Only the Elder of Dinglin [Zhixu] explained it thus: 'One observes with the life of wisdom.'"
Birth is like a fifth great element, like a sixth aggregate, like a seventh sense-faculty. Who, then, is a sentient being?
It is by means of sentient beings observing sentient beings that one then falsely perceives them as existing; thus, sentient beings are not the "sentient beings" of those whose life is wisdom.
These are merely sentient beings among sentient beings. That which is called "sentient beings among sentient beings" is itself not a sentient being;

yet it is precisely what is called a "sentient being. Thus, upon hearing this Dharma, if one can awaken to the nature and characteristics of one's own original essence, why would one not give rise to faith?
When one observes sentient beings with the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), seeing them as non-existent, how could one speak of "delivering sentient beings"?
It is said: "Sentient beings exist as sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not exist. The life of wisdom has no sentient beings, yet sentient beings are not non-existent.
For this reason, one delivers sentient beings."
The Great Wisdom Chan Master said: "This matter is not comprised of all names and categories. Why do you not answer with words of reality? [The other] replied:
"How could one carve empty space into the form of a Buddha? How could one say that empty space is blue, yellow, red, or white? As Vimalakīrti said:

Even if one were to debate face-to-face for a lifetime, there may be those who cannot distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. What is the reason for this?
It is because, at the moment of life and death, he was so transcendent and self-possessed; thus, the loftiness and subtlety of his lifelong cultivation can be known. What a pity!
There was no one to succeed him. Master [Hui]ji and Chan Master Yunhuo of Xifeng were brothers.
Chan Master Fanzheng, the second-generation successor at Baizhang Mountain, was a high disciple of Dazhi. His predecessor once recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* without disclosing his name;
he was thus called the "Nirvāṇa Monk. While residing at Chengfa Monastery, Master [Hui]ji’s contribution was the greatest.
He was one who caused the multitude to open the fields [of practice] and expounded the Great Meaning; he was indeed a Master. Huangbo, Guling, and other great beings all honored him.
The Tang literatus Wu Yihuang composed his stele inscription with great detail, and the calligraphy by Liu Gongquan is unsurpassed in antiquity and modern times.
Furthermore, the entry for Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) is also linked to Mazu’s Dharma lineage.
To place him in the line of succession is an error. Upon examining the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage), we find Weizheng and Fazheng;
yet, while the generations of Baizhang can be counted, Mingjiao merely saw their names and was unable to distinguish between them, so he preserved both.
Now, one should take the Liu stele as authoritative.
An ancient Buddha verse says: "Suppose a person digs up earth from a road and a private individual fashions it into an image.
A fool says the image has come into being; a wise person says it is merely road earth. Later, when the official wishes to travel, he takes the image and fills the road with it.

The image originally had neither birth nor extinction; the road is likewise neither new nor old. Another verse says: "When various forms and minds appear, they are like the relief patterns on gold and silver. The gold remains constant amidst its differences."

It is called "arising," yet it is simultaneous with gold, having no priority or posteriority. Therefore, Mañjuśrī said: "All the virtuous deeds in this assembly have never been performed from the very beginning;
all phenomena are likewise equal to the prior limit (pūrvakoṭi). Thus, at the very moment they are being performed, there is no performing."

Because there is no agent, that which should be done at a given time is not done. Because there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one may proceed freely through the myriad phenomena, always abiding in the limit of non-arising.
Thus one knows that a magnet never attracts iron, and ignorance does not condition the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Master Pang’s verse at the time of his death says: "Empty flowers fall into shadows; a mirage turns into waves. Master Yongming sighed: [and so forth].
Tasting the meaning of these words, it is said: "This does not fall into the views of existence or non-existence; it wonderfully captures the essence of non-arising.
Students should contemplate this deeply. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, some say that while earth is solid, the mind has no physical form or substance; both are [empty]."
This is false. For this reason, the Buddha taught that the power of the mind constitutes the great practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus, he could scatter this great earth into subtle atoms. Because the earth possesses color, fragrance, taste, and touch, and is heavy, it has no agency of its own.
Water, having less fragrance, excels the earth in its activity. Fire, having less fragrance and taste, excels water in its momentum. Wind has less color and fragrance [than fire].
Because it has flavor, the activity of fire is superior. Because the mind is free from these four matters, its power for what it undertakes is great.
Furthermore, because the mind is bound by many afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), the power of the mind is made to have outflows (*sāsrava*).

Although a wholesome mind lacks afflictions, its power is likewise slight because the mind grasps at the characteristics (*nimitta*) of various phenomena. Although the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the two vehicles does not grasp at characteristics, because of [their] wisdom...

Wisdom is limited; furthermore, when emerging from the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), the six sense faculties follow worldly conventions to differentiate and grasp the characteristics of phenomena, and thus do not exhaust the power of the mind.
The wisdom of the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas is immeasurable and boundless; they constantly abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
One makes no distinction between the world and nirvāṇa; the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is in fact not different.
It is only that there are degrees of excellence in wisdom. One who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately pure and unimpeded.
In a single thought-moment, they can disperse all the great trichiliocosm lands throughout the ten directions—lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—including their earths and mountains.
Because the mountain is as minute as a mote of dust, one knows that the mind possesses such great power. Sentient beings are separated by delusion and do not realize this themselves.

My vow is that those who hear this Dharma shall accord with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and practice for themselves, so that they may realize the essence of awakening is originally pure.
This is not a difficulty involving strenuous effort; it is simply a matter of focusing the mind. Now, my home mountain pervades the ten directions...
Now that you have sufficient clothing and food to sustain you for the rest of your life, and have already escaped all that is worthy of human anxiety, if you do not take this to heart,
is it not to turn your back on the grace and virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
Chan Master Jingfushun was a native of Western Sichuan. Possessing far-reaching insight, he was diligent and devoted in his conduct;
the junior monks of the monastic community all revered him as their mother. He received the Dharma from Old Huanglong.

In the past, he left Sichuan to travel together with Yuan Tong Nan, and subsequently spent a long time roaming with Da Jue Lian. One who praised his portrait said: "He traveled together with Nan, and [stayed] with Lian."

He lived together [with his teacher] and received the Dharma from Nan, becoming Nan’s eldest son. However, his karmic conditions were meager; all the monasteries where he resided were small ones in remote regions.
Scholars who passed by his gate were unable to recognize him, yet the Master remained transcendent and self-contented, regarding the worldly realm as mere motes of dust passing before his eyes.
At over eighty years of age, he passed away while seated on Mount Xiangcheng, his countenance appearing exactly as it had during his lifetime. He was born to the Pan family...
When Shouting was about to pass away, he sent someone to invite Yan to come and bid him farewell. When Yan arrived, the Master had already departed.
He had left behind many verses for the multitude, all of which were words of virtue. One verse said: "In summer, everyone fans themselves;
In winter, they fill the stove with charcoal. If one can fully understand this, The ignorance of kalpas will vanish this very moment."
Furthermore, he composed a verse on Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman, saying: Zhaozhou asked the way; the old woman replied, "Go straight ahead like this.

Everyone says she was "tested and exposed," yet the old woman leaves you with no place to clear your name. May those who share the Way raise this together. He also composed a verse on Huanglong’s Three Barriers, saying:
The clouds disperse over the long river, and the waters flow vast and deep; Suddenly a wild wind arises, and the waves surge high.
"Unaware of the profound and subtle meaning of the fisherman’s house, one merely tosses about amidst the waves and storms. It is also said: "A Persian from the South Sea enters the Great Tang;
if there is someone who recognizes the jewel, they will deliberate upon it. At times it is cheap, at times it is precious;

when the sun reaches the western peak, its shadow grows long. It is further said: "The Old Monk Huanglong has a saying regarding his 'birth affinity' (shengyuan); I, this mountain monk, have inherited his lineage."
"Eh! Today I shall raise one for you; I raise a cat for you, which is uniquely skilled at catching mice.

Zhu Xianmu Shiying, while formerly serving as an official in Nanchang, became acquainted with Yun’an. Not long after, he was transferred to Jiangdong to oversee grain transport and sent a letter inquiring about the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma.
Yun’an replied to him, saying: "I am honored by your letter inquiring about the Buddha-dharma. As for the Buddha-dharma..."
The ultimate subtlety is non-dual. However, as long as one has not reached this subtlety, there will inevitably be distinctions of long and short.
If one truly reaches this subtlety, then the person who awakens to the mind knows their own mind as it truly is: fundamentally and ultimately a Buddha.
They are truly sovereign, truly peaceful and happy, truly liberated, and truly pure; in their daily life, they employ only their own mind, for it is their own mind that undergoes transformation.
Transformation! Seize it and use it; do not inquire whether it is right or wrong. If you conceive thoughts or engage in deliberation, it is already not so.
Without conceiving thoughts, everything is authentically true; everything is luminously wondrous. Everything is like a lotus flower that remains unstained by water.

Therefore, by deluding one's own mind, one becomes a sentient being; by awakening to one's own mind, one becomes a Buddha. Thus, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, and Buddhas are themselves sentient beings.

It is due to delusion and awakening that there is "this" and "that. As for scholars today, many do not believe in their own minds, do not awaken to their own minds, and thus fail to obtain the luminous and wondrous enjoyment of their own minds, nor the peace and liberation of their own minds.

Outside the mind, they falsely conceive of Chan and the Way, falsely establish what is extraordinary, and falsely give rise to grasping and rejecting; even if they practice, they fall into the meditations of non-Buddhists or the Two Vehicles.
The words of Yun’an regarding the severance of the realm of views were intended to remedy the defects of a particular time;
nevertheless, their essential meaning is so clear that it can illuminate the obscurity of those who are ignorant. Therefore, I have privately recorded them.
Chan Master Daben was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Huilin Chan Monastery within the Great Xiangguo Temple.

As he was about to be led for an audience, the relevant officials had him practice the ceremonial protocols for several days. When Emperor Shen宗 appeared before him in the private hall, the Master, upon seeing him, simply offered the traditional "Mountain Cry" (shanhū).
The Emperor immediately hurried to the hall and offered him a seat. The Master proceeded to the couch, placed his feet on the footstool, and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

The attendants looked at one another in astonishment, yet the Master remained composed. When the tea was served, he raised the cup and drank deeply, then swirled it about. The Emperor asked, "In which monastery did you receive your formal training?"
He replied, "Chengtian Yong'an. This was indeed the Yong'an Cloister of Chengtian Temple in Suzhou. The Emperor was greatly pleased and conversed with him for a very long time.
After he had taken his leave, the Emperor watched him depart and said to those around him, "A truly blessed monk. An attendant asked: [Why did you say that?]
When asked by the official, "How did you see the Master? he replied, "We simply drank tea and conversed. His natural endowment was pure and refined;
his speech was concise and direct. He was truly transcendent and worthy of emulation.
The Daoist Ke Fu of Zhuo Prefecture met Linji, whose sharp wit and eloquence were of a transcendent caliber.

Ke Fu, noting that the Gate of the Patriarchs possessed the "Four Kinds of Critical Examination" (si liaojian) as the essential core of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' teachings, composed a verse to elucidate them, saying: "To seize the person but not the environment—this very condition carries its own confusion.
If you wish to seek the profound meaning, your deliberation will only lead to blame. The dragon pearl’s radiance is brilliant; the shadow of the moon and cassia is wavering."
Sa. To perceive the essence as undifferentiated is still to remain caught in the net. When the object is taken away but not the person, where is the truth in following words?
To ask about Chan is for Chan to be a delusion; to investigate principle is for principle to be distant. The sun shines and the cold light fades; the mountains are far and the green hues fresh.
Even if one attains profound realization, it is but dust in the eye. When both person and environment are simultaneously stripped away, this is the original true command.

To act—whether regarding Buddhas or Patriarchs—is to speak of the sentiments of sages and ordinary folk; to attempt this is like encountering a "blowing-feather" sword, yet it is as if meeting a blind man in the woods.
To advance further and seek a wondrous encounter is to deliberately sever one's own vital spirit.

When person and environment are both unassailable, when deliberation is free from bias, when host and guest do not differ in their speech, and when the principle of question and answer is complete, one tramples through the moon in the clear pool and pierces the azure void.
Heaven! One cannot clarify its wondrous function; one remains submerged in the unconditioned (wu-yan).

Chan Master Dongshan Wuben composed the "Standards and Essentials of the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject" and further wrote verses himself to be appended below them, saying: "The Center within the Deviant:

Before the moon becomes bright at the beginning of the third watch, Do not be surprised that we meet yet do not recognize one another; Hidden deep, I still harbor the resentment of days past. "The Deviant..."
Centered and Upright. At dawn’s break, an old woman encounters an ancient mirror; clearly face-to-face, there is nothing else. Do not further lose your head by still recognizing the reflection.
Coming from the Center: within non-existence there is a path that emerges from the dust. One need only avoid touching the taboo name of the present moment.
He surpasses even the "tongue-cutting" talent of former dynasties. Reaching the ultimate within the partial: when two blades clash, there is no need to avoid;

a true master is like a lotus in the fire, naturally possessing a spirit that pierces the heavens. Reaching the ultimate within the simultaneous: not falling into existence or non-existence, who would dare harmonize with this?
Everyone desires to escape the ordinary flow, yet when brought back to the point, they sit amidst the burning coals. Linji and Dongshan—the two [schools].

The essential characteristics of our school must manifest the Great Dharma; yet, in the transmission and copying of these verses by worldly practitioners, many have altered them to suit their own private interests, thereby losing the intent of the former masters.
I lament this in secret. I have now recorded the ancient edition here to correct the errors found in various transmissions.
Chan Master Baoben Yuan was solitary and steadfast; his character was exceptionally noble, and his deportment was dignified and grave. He would sit upright throughout the entire day.

Among the disciples of Chan Master Nan, he alone was able to emulate the Master’s conduct and hidden virtues. When the Master first began to propagate the Dharma, a letter from his dharma-heir arrived.
Upon seeing the monk’s name, Master Nan remarked, "I had almost forgotten this monk," and said to the messenger:
"I do not wish to open the letter yet; you may have someone come in person to see this old monk. The special envoy returned with his mission. The Master immediately packed his belongings and set out.
Upon reaching Yuzhang, he heard that National Teacher Nanyue had passed away, so he stayed there in deep lamentation. Just then, the elder Huitang came out of the city to meet him.

After conversing with him, Huitang marveled at his qualities, regretting only that he had not lived to see the Senior Teacher (Nanyue). The Master’s spiritual influence spread throughout Eastern Wu. People...
Those who returned to him were as numerous as clouds. Once, when he had gone out to beg for food, they carried him back on a boat.

At night, there were robbers; the boatmen cried out in terror, and blades flashed before them. The Master sat calmly and composedly. He spoke slowly, saying, "I offer everything I possess as a gift. One must not take a human life.
When the robbers had departed at dawn, people came to inspect the boat, thinking the Master was dead, yet his countenance—
His spirit was as serene and concentrated as on other days. He was able to remain so detached and free from entanglement when facing life and death or fortune and calamity.
Chan Master Hongzhun of Yanqing was a native of Guilin. He had studied under National Teacher Nan for many years; his natural disposition was pure and profound.
He never once acted in opposition to others. Upon hearing of another's virtue, he regarded it as his own; a radiant joy would well up from between his brows.
When hearing of another's evil, he would invariably join his palms and strike the air as if in repentance, causing all who saw him to laugh at him.
Yet his sincerity was such that it remained consistent from beginning to end. In his later years, he did not take charge of monastic affairs, but made his home at Hanxi.

He was over eighty years old at the time. Throughout his life, he had no other pursuits day or night; beyond sleeping and eating, he did nothing but chant the *brahmanī* sounds and offer praises to Avalokiteśvara.
When the time of his death arrived, while all his disciples and followers had gone to attend a meal for the donors, only a single servant remained.
The Master took up his *qing* (stone chime) and sat before the shrine of the local deity, reciting the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra* once.

He bid farewell and sat down peacefully with his eyes closed. For three days he did not shift. Villagers came to view him, standing shoulder-to-shoulder like a wall. Suddenly, the Master opened his eyes and smiled;
he had them sit on the ground. After a short while, the disciples returned. The Master called for one to stand at his right and grasped his hand as if it were cooked rice.
For a long time he remained silent, then he looked up and departed. His countenance did not change; his cheeks were as rosy as when he was alive. Thus passed the Way.
A secular image of him was fashioned and enshrined in a niche. I once visited his hermitage to pay my respects and gaze upon it;

I marveled that throughout his life he had practiced with such hidden virtue and subtle application, never seeking to seek recognition from the world, yet at the moment of death and rebirth, he was able to transcend it so completely.

Truly a great man! Although Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and contemplate all phenomena as being like the nature of empty space, they still realize this mindlessness gradually.
Even upon reaching the tenth stage, two types of delusion (*moha*) still remain; it is only after entering the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) that [these are fully eliminated].

Thus, a portion of ignorance remains unexhausted, like a wisp of smoke; yet one is still able to perform repentance. Judging by this, according to the *Fan-zan* (Praise of Brahmā), is he not also one who governs himself?
When National Teacher Nanyue resided at Jicui, one night while he sat in meditation, a light illuminated his dwelling. He cautioned his attendant not to speak of it outside.
After Master Song Mingjiao had passed away, his body was cremated; his cranial bone, eyes, teeth, tongue, ear-pilus, male organ, and rosary remained uncorrupted.
As the World-Honored One had said: "A bhikṣu’s physical body remains uncorrupted, emitting the light of stainless wisdom."
This is due to the power of the merit of their roots of goodness and the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;

therefore, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they must be pure both internally and externally. Those two great elders are now within the reach of our own ears and eyes, not belonging to another age.
That they alone were so exceptionally sublime—is this not clear evidence of the practice they pursued throughout their lives? I once composed two verses, saying: "The Tathāgata..."
Through the power of merit, both internally and externally one is entirely pure. When thoughts arise, do not follow them; naturally the mind will be free from affliction.

One’s form becomes equal to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and through the Way, one brings about the protection of humans and devas. With pure precepts, one gains the blessings of humans and devas; with an empty mind, one is identical to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
I once visited the stupa of Chan Master Yunfeng Yue with several monks. As we rose from our prostrations, I patted it and asked, "Is he alive?
Is he dead? After a long silence, I answered myself: "One cannot topple this stupa. A monk beside me remarked, "Today’s occasion is exactly like the circumstances of Daowu.
Thereupon, I composed a verse to show him: "If you do not know, then ask; If you have not seen, then look."
[This] has been investigated. When perfection is manifest before one, why need it be spoken of further? This adamantine body—birth, death, sickness, and old age—is like a stupa before one's eyes;
it cannot be toppled.
Master Yan of Nanzhan Rock was traditionally said to be an emanation of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. His miraculous traces were numerous, and he has his own biography;
however, that biography does not record the name of the master from whom he received the Dharma, referring to him only as "Xifeng.
Xifeng was located at Zhenmiao in Luling. At that time, there was a Chan Master Yunhuo, who was a senior disciple of Master Shenxian.
Shenjian was a Yunmen lineage master of such caliber that, at that time, there were no "dragons and elephants" (outstanding masters) who could surpass him.

Only Chan Master Ming of Qingliang was his equal in fame; they were known as the two elders, Shen and Ming. Master Yan often instructed people using verses, and at the end of each verse he invariably inscribed four characters:
"Zeng yi zhi zhong" (Presented to Yizhong). No one in the world could fathom their meaning. At the time of his death, he said to the assembly: "You..."
"You should know that this wondrous nature is vast and empty; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing. It manifests coming and going, yet what more is there to doubt?
Today I am born into this world, and now is precisely the time. He then lay down on his right side. I said: "When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he said:"
I was born on this day; now is precisely the time for it.
I once traveled through Eastern Wu and stayed at Jingci Temple on West Lake. In the temple’s main hall, two pavilions were constructed along the eastern and western corridors;
they were exceedingly lofty and magnificent. An elderly monk of the temple told me that Master Yongming [Yanshou] had, by means of the Xianshou and Cien...
"En, the three schools of Tiantai [clashed] like ice and charcoal, failing to reach a comprehensive understanding.

He invited disciples who were refined in the dharma and its principles to extensively read the ocean of meanings within the two pavilions and engage in mutual debate. The Master then used the standards of the Mind School to adjudicate them.
Furthermore, he compiled sixty Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras by the virtuous and renowned masters of India and this land."

He spoke of three hundred families to substantiate the principle of Mind-Only. He composed one hundred fascicles of a work transmitted to the world, titled the *Zhongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source).
Its benefit as a gift of the Dharma may be called vast and extraordinary. Today, there is no famous mountain in the land where this does not exist;
yet among scholars, there are those who have never once unrolled its pages throughout their entire lives, merely eating their fill and remaining idle.
Sleeping; their idle talk is merely groundless. Is this called repaying the Buddha’s kindness, or is it rather incurring the Buddha’s debt?
Chan Master Tong’an Cha composed the *Ten Profound Discourses* (*Shi xuantan*), greatly propagating the essential meaning of the "wondrous embrace" within the "correct center.

His words were exquisite and elegant, illuminating the monastic community. However, as the years have passed, much of the authenticity has been lost. What is now recorded in the *Transmission of the Lamp* bears the title—
The accounts differ. In *Duguan suobian wujia zongpai* (The Five Houses’ Lineages Compiled by Duguan), the genealogies are recorded quite in detail.
I once obtained an old edition of it; it differs only slightly from what is contained in *Wujia zongpai*.

According to the *Chuan deng lu*, this master was the successor of Jiufeng Qian, yet Duguan designates him as the son of Yunju Ying. I do not understand how Duguan could have obtained such [information].
Is this true? However, it was not long after the passing of Master Qingliang Fayen that these verses of praise were composed.
Since their narrative follows what is recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), the theories of the Five Houses must also be viewed with suspicion.

As for the verses on the Ten Mysteries (*shí xuán*), one should examine their titles regarding their sequence; they were all composed as a continuous series. The first five stanzas demonstrate the essential principles, while the latter five stanzas...
One should practice this. However, although the eight verses all consist of two-character titles and their meanings are interconnected, the phrasing rises and falls in a repetitive pattern.

The first is titled "Verses on the Mind-Seal" (Xinyin Jì), and the last states: "Even a mindless state still leaves behind a further barrier. Therefore, he also composed the "Verses on the Patriarchal Meaning" (Zuyì Jì), the first line of which says:

"How could the true mechanism fall into the realm of existence or non-existence? For this reason, he also composed the "Verses on the True Mechanism" (Zhēnjī Jì), the first line of which says: "How could it..."

Because it creates entanglements with the deluded faculties of the mundane world, he further composed the "Verses on the Difference from the Mundane. Within it, he says: "The three vehicles are distinguished by forceful naming";
thus, he also composed the "Succession of the Three Vehicles. This is the essential point he intended to show. Reaching the sixth [section], it is called the "Verse on Returning to the Source.
At the end, he asks: "How shall the melody of the 'Song of Returning Home' be sung? Thus, he further composed the "Song of Returning Home."

The verse concludes: "There is not a single thing further to offer to the Honored Hall. This constitutes sitting within the position of correctness; yet, if one merely settles there, it is not yet the subtle embrace.

Therefore, one must again effect a turning of the faculty. If the faculty is subtly grasped, the fundamental source is lost. To still harbor views and cognitions is called the "great illness. Therefore, one must again effect a shifting of the position.
This shifting of the position is what is meant by "acting within the midst of different categories. When different categories are entirely biased, one must nevertheless return [to the source].
It is correct. This is so that the vital pulse may not be severed; thus, after one color has passed, this is intended to cause [the practitioner] to tread upon it.
The Five Houses of the Zen school also say: "After one color has passed, there is merely the difference of dust; it is simply that within the dust there is difference."

Chan Master Nanshan’s demeanor was solemn and profound; no one could fathom the extent of his capacity. Consequently, many of his disciples were luminous, magnificent, and outstanding, their reputations esteemed throughout the monastic community.
There were those who never in their entire lives witnessed him break into a smile. I have heard that those who are excessive in righteousness (yi) are deficient in benevolence (ren);
this is the way of the teacher. The Master was revered but not intimate. Those who are excessive in benevolence are deficient in righteousness.
This is to be close to the Way. To be close to one's kin yet not to revere them—was this not the intention of Duke Nan?
In the village of Zui, there was a mad monk named Jiedao who resided in a settlement and was drunk every day.

Nevertheless, his speech was strange and marvelous, such that no one in the world could determine whether he was an ordinary man or a sage. When someone gave him wine and asked him to compose a sacrificial inscription himself, Jie responded:
The voice said: "O virtuous one, you were born in Jambudvīpa; though you were free from anger and envy, you loved to drink wine until you fell down in the streets and lay upon the roads.
Yet, you have been reborn in Tuṣita Heaven precisely because at that time you ceased drinking wine. Why is this?
Within the Pure Land, there is no wine to be purchased."
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* takes non-abiding as its central tenet.

Since non-abiding is its tenet, it would seem appropriate that all its discourse should sweep away appearances and shatter existence, such that not even a speck of dust could be established. Yet, half the sūtra praises the superiority of merit.

Furthermore, the practice of observing precepts and cultivating merit are matters of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Nevertheless, when the World-Honored One answers those who can give rise to faith in this sūtra, he necessarily...

Who was this person? Lord Wang Wen (Wang Anshi) retired from the相位 (Prime Minister’s office) and returned to live in seclusion at Mount Zhongshan. Whenever he encountered a monastic, he would invariably inquire into their mastery of the Way and its teachings;

he was particularly well-versed in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. He once composed his own commentary on its meaning; his prose was concise yet unrestrained, omitting the prolixities of other masters while being detailed where necessary.
The Master’s concise [teachings] cannot be fathomed by anyone who has not recognized the subtle. He would often say:

"Nowadays, those who read this scripture see that what it teaches—the wondrous luminosity of fundamental awakening (*benjue*) and the luminous subtlety of the nature of awakening (*xingjue*)—reveals that the arising of the body, the sensory faculties, and the physical world does not transcend my own mind.
Yet, I privately doubt this: while Mount Zhongshan is but a single gathering place of mountains and rivers, how is it that one can roam within them without..."
Suppose there are a thousand people. How could it be that these thousand people share one and the same external object within their minds?
For instance, if among these thousand people one were suddenly to die, how could these mountains and rivers ever perish along with him?

Since the person departs while the object remains, the principle of the arising of the mountains, rivers, and great earth as described in the sutras would be untenable. How, then, can this be reconciled to accord with the Buddha’s original intent?
Shimen Hong Juefan’s *Línjiān Lù*, Part Two (Concluding)
